Identification and Inference of Bi-directional Causal Effects in Mendelian Randomization without Instrument Selection

Liyuan Mo*    Qingyuan Zhao
Abstract

Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects. Bidirectional MR usually uses two reversed unidirectional analyses, but feedback can invalidate instruments in at least one direction and induce correlated pleiotropy. We model both traits as a stable cyclic system and estimate both directional effects from GWAS summary data without instrument selection or a prespecified valid-instrument subset. After LD score normalisation, marginal associations form a heteroscedastic noisy independent component analysis model, assuming the variants’ direct effects on the two traits are independent. If those effects are non-Gaussian, this identifies the total-effect matrix up to scaling and permutation; no-self-feedback and stability of the system further resolve these ambiguities. We develop an estimator based on noise-adjusted second- and fourth-order moments, avoiding inversion of the high-dimensional linkage disequilibrium matrix and having computational cost linear in the number of variants. Under weak local dependence, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and validity of a chromosome-respecting moving block bootstrap. Simulations show negligible bias, generally reliable interval coverage, and higher rejection rates for nonzero directional effects than focusing-based tests. Three real-data applications illustrate how joint analysis of feedback systems can yield causal decompositions differing from two separate unidirectional analyses.

Keywords: Correlated pleiotropy; Feedback systems; GWAS; Independent component analysis; LD score.

1 Introduction

Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instrumental variables, or “natural experiments,” to infer causal effects from observational data (Davey Smith and Ebrahim,, 2003; Davey Smith and Hemani,, 2014; Burgess and Thompson,, 2015; Sanderson et al.,, 2022). The increasing availability of genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics has made MR an important tool for studying complex traits and has led to its widespread use in health and social science (Hemani et al.,, 2018; Richmond and Davey Smith,, 2022). Over the past decade, substantial methodological work has developed estimators robust to horizontal pleiotropy under assumptions such as InSIDE (INstrument Strength Independent of Direct Effect) or majority/plurality conditions (Bowden et al.,, 2015; Bowden et al.,, 2016; Kang et al.,, 2016; Guo et al.,, 2018; Zhao et al.,, 2020). MR has also been extended to multivariable settings (Sanderson et al.,, 2019; Wang et al.,, 2021), mediation and time-varying settings (Wu et al.,, 2025), nonlinear exposure-outcome relationships (Staley and Burgess,, 2017), and within-family designs that reduce bias from population structure and familial effects (Brumpton et al.,, 2020; Tudball et al.,, 2022).

Despite these advances, most MR methods prespecify an exposure-outcome ordering and select variants associated with the designated exposure as instruments. However, the causal direction for many pairs of biological or behavioural traits is uncertain a priori, and reciprocal effects are often scientifically plausible (Davey Smith and Hemani,, 2014; Richmond and Davey Smith,, 2019; Sanderson et al.,, 2022). A common practice is to reverse the role of the two traits and fit two separate unidirectional analyses, but this does not estimate one coherent feedback system in general. The two analyses may use different selected variants, significance thresholds and effective linkage disequilibrium (LD) structures. More importantly, a variant selected for one direction may primarily affect the outcome and be associated with the exposure via reverse causal pathway, resulting in an invalid instrumental variable and non-identifiability due to correlated pleiotropy (Morrison et al.,, 2020; Wang et al.,, 2021; Darrous et al.,, 2021; Li and Ye,, 2025). Direction-specific variant selection also poses methodological and practical challenges. Estimates may be affected by winner’s curse or post-selection bias, and conclusions can depend on the GWAS dataset used for SNP selection, significance threshold and LD-clumping parameters (Wang and Han,, 2021; Ma et al.,, 2023; Jiang et al.,, 2023; Swerdlow et al.,, 2016; Boehm and Zhou,, 2022). For highly polygenic traits, selection can discard many weak but collectively informative signals (Boyle et al.,, 2017; Visscher et al.,, 2017; Zhao et al.,, 2019). Moreover, selection on observed marginal associations conditions changes the distribution of true genetic effects and can invalidate identifying assumptions like InSIDE in bidirectional analyses.

Several methods have considered causal orientation or explicitly bi-directional relationships. Steiger-type procedures orient a putative one-directional relationship by comparing explained variation (Hemani et al.,, 2017; Xue and Pan,, 2020). Wang et al., (2021) developed a test for causal direction by investigating a bimodal structure in a pseudo-likelihood function. Darrous et al., (2021) proposed a parametric model with a latent heritable confounder and estimated the structural parameters by maximizing a complex likelihood function. Li and Ye, (2025) developed a test for bi-directional causal effects by selecting a “focused” set of instruments for each direction. Other work has studied identification and inference under plurality-type, covariance heterogeneity, or valid-instrument-set conditions (Xue and Pan,, 2022; Li et al.,, 2024; Xie et al.,, 2024). These approaches make important progress, but identification typically remains linked to a parametric effect distribution or to the existence of variants that behave as valid instruments in at least one direction.

1.1 Our approach and contributions

We briefly review the model used in this article and refer the reader to Section 2 for further details. We model the two traits as a stable simultaneous system with structural coefficients matrix

𝐁=(0β12β210),\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta_{12}\\ \beta_{21}&0\end{pmatrix},

where βj​k\beta_{jk} is the direct causal effect of trait kk on trait jj. We will refer to 𝐀=(𝐈2−𝐁)−1\mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}, which admits a Neumann-series expansion 𝐀=𝐈2+𝐁+𝐁2+⋯\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}_{2}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B}^{2}+\cdots if 𝐁\mathbf{B} is (Schur) stable, as the “total-effect” matrix. Let NN be the number of genetic variants. We assume the marginal GWAS summary data 𝚪^∈ℝN×2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2} (Γ^j​k\widehat{\Gamma}_{jk} is the GWAS effect of variant jj on trait kk) satisfy

𝚪^=𝐑​𝜶​𝐀⊤+𝐄,\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}+\mathbf{E}, (1.1)

where 𝐑∈ℝN×N\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is the linkage disequilibrium (LD) correlation matrix, and 𝜶∈ℝN×2\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2} contains variant-specific direct genetic effects, 𝐄\mathbf{E} is the GWAS sampling error with a known multivariate normal distribution. A similar formulation was used by Darrous et al., (2021). The formulation (1.1) allows every variant to have direct effects on both traits and does not require any particular variant, or any pre-specified subset, to satisfy the conventional exclusion restriction. Instead, for identification we rely on the key assumption that the genetic variants have independent direct effects on the two traits (two columns of 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} are independent); we term this the INdependent DIrect Effect (InDiE) assumption. Such independence does not exclude widespread pleiotropy but rules out systematic alignment of the direct genetic effects. It is related in spirit to the InSIDE assumption (Bowden et al.,, 2015) (and indeed reduces to InSIDE in uni-directional MR), but is imposed on the joint distribution of all variant-level direct genetic effects rather than on a selected set of instruments.

Our first main contribution is linking bi-directional MR with independent component analysis (ICA) (Comon,, 1994; Hyvärinen and Oja,, 2000). Under the InDiE assumption, the model in (1.1) admits a noisy ICA representation, with 𝐀\mathbf{A} as the mixing matrix and the LD-aggregated direct genetic effects as the latent source signals. It is well known that the mixing matrix in ICA is identifiable up to column rescaling and permutation if the source components are independent and at most one is Gaussian. Building on the ICA-based approach to identifying cyclic structural equation models developed by Lacerda et al., (2008), we show that these ambiguities can be resolved in our bi-directional MR setting: the unit-diagonal constraint on 𝐀−1=𝐈2−𝐁\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B} fixes the scaling, while stability of the simultaneous system selects the correct permutation.

Note that (1.1) is not a standard ICA model: LD creates local dependence across variants and GWAS sampling produces measurement error. This creates new challenges: direct inversion of the high-dimensional LD matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} is numerically unstable, and existing ICA methods do not allow heteroscedastic noise. We develop novel solutions to these challenges by using LD-score normalization to stabilize the LD-aggregated genetic signals and extending the popular JADE algorithm (Cardoso and Souloumiac,, 1993) to this noisy ICA setting. Because we do not attempt to remove the local dependence of GWAS marginal associations, our algorithm does not require the full LD matrix and has a computational complexity that is linear in the number of variants.

To quantify the uncertainty of our estimator of the structural coefficients in 𝐁\mathbf{B}, we use a moving block bootstrap (Lahiri,, 2003) that respects the genomic structure of the problem. We further develop an asymptotic theory that establishes the consistency and central limit theorem of the estimator and justifies moving block bootstrap under weak local dependence. In simulations, the proposed method has negligible bias and generally reliable coverage across a range of feedback, LD and signal-strength settings. It also shows higher statistical power for directional effects than the directional focusing procedures of Li and Ye, (2025) and is substantially faster than LHC-MR (Darrous et al.,, 2021). Three real-data applications further demonstrate how joint estimation of the simultaneous system can yield different conclusions from two separately reversed analyses.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the structural and summary-data models. Section 3 establishes identification of the bi-directional causal effects and develops the proposed estimator, including recovery of the causal matrix from the ICA representation. Section 4 gives the asymptotic theory and bootstrap inference. Sections 5 and 6 present the simulation studies and real-data applications, respectively, and Section 7 concludes. Additional numerical results, methodological details and proofs are provided in the Supplementary Material.

2 Bi-directional summary-data model

Let 𝐓=(T1,T2)⊤\mathbf{T}=(T_{1},T_{2})^{\top} denote the two traits and 𝐙=(Z1,…,ZN)⊤\mathbf{Z}=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{N})^{\top} the vector of centred and standardised genotypes at NN harmonised variants, with the variants ordered by chromosome and physical position. We assume 𝔼⁡(𝐙)=𝟎\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{0} and Cov⁡(𝐙)=𝐑\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{R}, where 𝐑\mathbf{R} is the LD correlation matrix. The observed data consist of the marginal GWAS association estimates for the two traits at these variants and their reported standard errors.

2.1 Cyclic structural model

We model the traits by the simultaneous system

𝐓=𝐁𝐓+𝜶⊤​𝐙+𝐔+𝜺,𝐁=(0β12β210).\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{T}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}+\mathbf{U}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\qquad\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta_{12}\\ \beta_{21}&0\end{pmatrix}. (2.1)

The zero diagonal of 𝐁\mathbf{B} encodes the no-self-feedback constraint, excluding direct causal effects of either trait on itself. The coefficient β12\beta_{12} is the causal effect from trait 2 to trait 1 and β21\beta_{21} is the effect from trait 1 to trait 2. The matrix 𝜶=(αj​k)∈ℝN×2\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_{jk})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2} contains the direct genetic effects before causal propagation, while 𝐔+𝜺\mathbf{U}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} collects non-genetic and trait-specific structural disturbances, respectively.

The formulation in (2.1) is a simultaneous-equation model for a feedback system. We impose the following stability condition.

Assumption 1 (Stability).

The bi-directional causal effects satisfy |β12​β21|<1|\beta_{12}\beta_{21}|<1.

Since 𝐁2=β12​β21​𝐈2\mathbf{B}^{2}=\beta_{12}\beta_{21}\mathbf{I}_{2}, Assumption 1 ensures that 𝐈2−𝐁\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B} is invertible and that the Neumann series converges:

(𝐈2−𝐁)−1=∑m=0∞𝐁m.(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\mathbf{B}^{m}.

Consequently, the cumulative effects of successive feedback remain finite, and the system has a unique stable equilibrium (Lauritzen and Richardson,, 2002; Hyttinen et al.,, 2012).

The stability condition also distinguishes between observationally equivalent structural representations. When both β12\beta_{12} and β21\beta_{21} are nonzero, the equations in (2.1) can be rearranged to give an alternative representation in which β12\beta_{12} is replaced by β21−1\beta_{21}^{-1} and β21\beta_{21} by β12−1\beta_{12}^{-1}. This rearrangement involves exchanging and rescaling the two structural equations. However, the product of the bi-directional causal effects in the alternative representation is (β12​β21)−1(\beta_{12}\beta_{21})^{-1}, whose absolute value exceeds one. The alternative representation is therefore excluded by Assumption 1.

Solving (2.1) for 𝐓\mathbf{T} yields the reduced-form representation

𝐓=𝐀​𝜶⊤​𝐙+𝐀⁡(𝐔+𝜺),𝐀:=(𝐈2−𝐁)−1=11−β12​β21​(1β12β211).\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{U}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}),\qquad\mathbf{A}:=(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}=\frac{1}{1-\beta_{12}\beta_{21}}\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta_{12}\\ \beta_{21}&1\end{pmatrix}. (2.2)

The matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} is the total-effect matrix, aggregating the direct and indirect effects propagated through the feedback system.

2.2 Marginal association model under LD

Assume genetic exogeneity with respect to the non-genetic disturbance, 𝔼⁡{𝐙​(𝐔+𝜺)⊤}=𝟎\mathbb{E}\{\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{U}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})^{\top}\}=\mathbf{0}. The matrix of marginal variant–trait associations then satisfies

𝚪=Cov⁡(𝐙,𝐓)=𝐑​𝜶​𝐀⊤.\boldsymbol{\Gamma}=\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{T})=\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}. (2.3)

Thus marginal associations combine LD aggregation of the direct genetic effects with propagation through the causal system.

Let 𝚪^\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}} and 𝐄\mathbf{E} denote the corresponding matrix of GWAS summary estimates and summary-statistic estimation errors. The observed model is

𝚪^=𝚪+𝐄=𝐑​𝜶​𝐀⊤+𝐄,𝐀=(𝐈2−𝐁)−1.\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}+\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}+\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}. (2.4)

The following working condition specifies the summary-statistic error model.

Assumption 2 (Summary-statistic error).

The error 𝐄\mathbf{E} is independent of 𝛂\boldsymbol{\alpha}. If 𝐞j⊤\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\top} is its jjth row, then 𝐞j∼ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺j)\mathbf{e}_{j}\sim\mathbb{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}). For non-overlapping two-sample studies, 𝚺j=diag⁡(σj​12,σj​22)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{j1}^{2},\sigma_{j2}^{2}), where σj​k\sigma_{jk} is the reported standard error. With sample overlap, a nonzero cross-trait error covariance may be incorporated when available.

The Gaussian approximation is standard for GWAS summary statistics (Zhao et al.,, 2020). The covariance 𝚺j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j} may vary across variants, and nearby summary-statistic errors may remain weakly dependent through LD.

The target in (2.4) is causal matrix 𝐁\mathbf{B}, whose estimation is complicated by latent nuisance quantities, LD-induced dependence, and heteroscedastic summary-statistic errors.

3 Identification and estimation

We identify the causal effects by exploiting the distributional structure of the direct genetic effects. LD-score normalisation first converts (2.4) into a noisy ICA model with mixing matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}. Standard ICA arguments identify this matrix up to scaling and permutation, while the no-self-feedback and stability constraints of the feedback system resolve these remaining ambiguities. We estimate the mixing matrix using noise-adjusted second- and fourth-order moments, and then recover the causal effects using the structural constraints of the feedback system.

Assumption 3 (Direct-effect distribution).

For 𝛂j⋅=(αj​1,αj​2)⊤\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot}=(\alpha_{j1},\alpha_{j2})^{\top}:

  1. (i)

    the vectors {𝜶j⋅}j=1N\{\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot}\}_{j=1}^{N} are independent and identically distributed across variants, and their two components are independent, with 𝔼(𝜶j⋅)=𝟎,Cov(𝜶j⋅)=𝐃α=diag(σα,12,σα,22)\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot})=\boldsymbol{0},\quad\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot})=\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{\alpha,1}^{2},\sigma_{\alpha,2}^{2}), where 0<σα,k2<∞0<\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{2}<\infty for k=1,2k=1,2;

  2. (ii)

    at most one component distribution is Gaussian.

The cross-trait independence in part (i) is the InDiE condition introduced in Section 1. It is imposed on the primitive direct genetic effects, not on the observed marginal associations, and allows both direct effects of a variant to be nonzero. Part (ii) is the standard non-Gaussianity requirement for ICA identification and accommodates many sparse and mixture-like genetic architectures. Further discussion is given in Supplementary Section S1.2.

3.1 LD-score normalisation and the noisy ICA representation

In the observed model (2.4), LD aggregates direct genetic effects across variants through 𝐑\mathbf{R}, while the total-effect matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} propagates these effects through the feedback system. Our interest is in 𝐀\mathbf{A}, rather than the direct effects at individual variants. LD aggregation makes the covariance of the aggregated effects depend on the local LD structure and induces dependence between neighbouring variants. Undoing LD aggregation by premultiplying the summary associations by 𝐑−1\mathbf{R}^{-1} would require inversion of a high-dimensional, potentially ill-conditioned matrix and would also transform the summary-statistic errors. We instead retain the marginal associations and use the covariance structure of the LD-aggregated effects to construct a normalised model.

For variant jj, let 𝐠j=∑r=1NRj​r𝜶r⋅\mathbf{g}_{j}=\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{r\cdot} denote its LD-aggregated direct-effect vector. Under Assumption 3, Cov⁡(𝐠j)=ℓj​𝐃α\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{g}_{j})=\ell_{j}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}, where ℓj=∑r=1NRj​r2\ell_{j}=\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{2} is the LD score of variant jj. Thus the variation in this covariance across variants is entirely captured by the scalar ℓj\ell_{j}. Scaling each marginal association by ℓj−1/2\ell_{j}^{-1/2} removes this factor from the covariance of the LD-aggregated effects without changing the mixing matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}.

Let 𝐃ℓ=diag⁡(ℓ1,…,ℓN)\mathbf{D}_{\ell}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{N}). The LD-score-normalised summary-data model is

𝐗=𝐃ℓ−1/2𝚪^=𝐒𝐀⊤+𝐄~,𝐒=𝐃ℓ−1/2𝐑𝜶,𝐄~=𝐃ℓ−1/2𝐄.\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{-1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}=\mathbf{S}\mathbf{A}^{\top}+\widetilde{\mathbf{E}},\qquad\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{-1/2}\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\alpha},\quad\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{-1/2}\mathbf{E}. (3.1)

For each variant j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N, the corresponding row model is

𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j,𝐬j=ℓj−1/2∑r=1NRj​r𝜶r⋅.\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j},\qquad\mathbf{s}_{j}=\ell_{j}^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{r\cdot}. (3.2)

This is a noisy independent component analysis (ICA) representation with heteroscedastic Gaussian errors: 𝐀\mathbf{A} is the common mixing matrix, 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} is the latent source vector, and 𝐞~j\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j} is the transformed summary-statistic error. The two coordinates of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} are independent because they are formed from the two independent columns of 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}; the error is independent of the source vector. Moreover,

Cov⁡(𝐬j)=𝐃α,Cov⁡(𝐞~j)=𝚺jld:=ℓj−1​𝚺j.\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{s}_{j})=\mathbf{D}_{\alpha},\qquad\operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}:=\ell_{j}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}. (3.3)

Consequently, the signal component 𝐀𝐬j\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j} has the common covariance 𝐑s:=𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤\mathbf{R}_{s}:=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}, whereas Cov⁡(𝐱j)=𝐑s+𝚺jld\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{j})=\mathbf{R}_{s}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}} may vary across variants. This common signal covariance provides the basis for noise-adjusted whitening in Section 3.4.

LD-score normalisation yields a common signal covariance across variants, but does not eliminate dependence across variants or ensure that the transformed observations are identically distributed. Neighbouring source vectors may share direct genetic effects through overlapping LD patterns, and their higher-order moments may differ despite their common covariance. The independence of the source components at each variant supports the ICA identification argument in Section 3.2, while estimation requires noise-adjusted moments and inference must accommodate local dependence. Further comparison with ordinary ICA is given in Supplementary Section S1.1.

3.2 Identification of the causal matrix

At any fixed variant index, the Gaussian error in (3.2) has known covariance and an everywhere nonzero characteristic function. Its contribution can therefore be deconvolved from the distribution of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}, identifying the distribution of 𝐀𝐬j\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}. The coordinates of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} are independent; moreover, if sj​ks_{jk} were Gaussian, Cramér’s decomposition theorem and Rj​j=1R_{jj}=1 would imply that the corresponding primitive direct-effect distribution is Gaussian. Assumption 3(ii) therefore ensures that at most one effective source is Gaussian. Thus, the usual ICA identifiability condition holds, and 𝐀\mathbf{A} is identified up to column scaling and permutation (Comon,, 1994; Hyvärinen et al.,, 2001). A formal statement is given in Supplementary Theorem S1.

It remains to use the structural form of the feedback system to remove the usual ICA ambiguities. Let

𝐖=𝐀−1=𝐈2−𝐁=(1−β12−β211).\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\beta_{12}\\ -\beta_{21}&1\end{pmatrix}.

If ICA returns 𝐀𝐏𝐃\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}, with permutation matrix 𝐏\mathbf{P} and nonsingular diagonal matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D}, its inverse differs from 𝐖\mathbf{W} by row permutation and scaling. Since 𝐖\mathbf{W} has unit diagonal, we consider the two possible row orderings and normalise each to have unit diagonal, provided that both diagonal entries are nonzero. When both causal effects are nonzero, exchanging the sources and rescaling them leaves the observed ICA model unchanged but gives the alternative causal matrix

𝐁swap=(01/β211/β120),β12swap​β21swap=(β12​β21)−1.\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{swap}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/\beta_{21}\\ 1/\beta_{12}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\beta_{12}^{\mathrm{swap}}\beta_{21}^{\mathrm{swap}}=(\beta_{12}\beta_{21})^{-1}.

Under Assumption 1, the alternative product has absolute value greater than one and is therefore excluded by stability. If either causal effect is zero, the swapped row ordering has a zero diagonal entry before row-normalisation and is inadmissible. Thus the structural constraints select a unique causal matrix from the ICA equivalence class.

The resolution of the ICA scaling and permutation ambiguities builds on the identification approach for cyclic structural models of Lacerda et al., (2008). Combining this structural recovery with identification of the mixing matrix in the noisy ICA representation of LD-score-normalised GWAS summary statistics yields the following result for bi-directional MR.

Theorem 1 (Identification of the bi-directional causal effects).

Under Assumptions 1-3, the causal matrix 𝐁\mathbf{B}, and hence (β12,β21)(\beta_{12},\beta_{21}), is uniquely identified from the distribution of the summary statistics together with the summary-error covariance information.

The identification uses the joint distribution of all variant-level direct genetic effects rather than a pleiotropy-free subset. This has a further consequence for variant selection.

3.3 Variant selection and source independence

The InDiE condition ensures independence between the two source components in (3.2). However, instrument selection based on marginal associations conditions on mixtures of these components rather than on the direct genetic effects themselves. To examine its implications, consider the noise-free component 𝐱j(0)=𝐀𝐬j\mathbf{x}_{j}^{(0)}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}. If a variant is selected when ℰj={𝐱j(0)∈𝒞}\mathcal{E}_{j}=\{\mathbf{x}_{j}^{(0)}\in\mathcal{C}\}, the corresponding event in source coordinates is {𝐬j∈𝐀−1𝒞}\{\mathbf{s}_{j}\in\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathcal{C}\}. Such conditioning can induce dependence between the source components.

Proposition 1 (Selection and source independence).

Let 𝐬j=(sj​1,sj​2)⊤\mathbf{s}_{j}=(s_{j1},s_{j2})^{\top} have independent components and let 𝐱j(0)=𝐀𝐬j\mathbf{x}_{j}^{(0)}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}, where 𝐀\mathbf{A} is nonsingular. Consider a selection event ℰj={𝐱j(0)∈𝒞}\mathcal{E}_{j}=\{\mathbf{x}_{j}^{(0)}\in\mathcal{C}\} with 0<ℙ⁡(ℰj)<10<\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{j})<1. If 𝐀−1​𝒞\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathcal{C} is not a Cartesian product of two measurable sets, up to a null set under the distribution of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j}, then sj​1​⟂⟂sj​2|ℰjs_{j1}\not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp s_{j2}\mid\mathcal{E}_{j}.

For example, selecting variants according to ℰj={|xj​1(0)|>c}\mathcal{E}_{j}=\{|x_{j1}^{(0)}|>c\} amounts to conditioning on {|A11sj​1+A12sj​2|>c}\{|A_{11}s_{j1}+A_{12}s_{j2}|>c\}. When both source components enter the marginal association, the selection region is generally not a Cartesian product, and conditioning can induce dependence between the components. For noisy GWAS summary statistics, selection on observed associations similarly reweights the source distribution by a generally non-factorisable selection probability; see Supplementary Section S1.2. Thus, direction-specific instrument selection can violate the source independence underlying ICA identification, beyond simply discarding weak but collectively informative variants or introducing sensitivity to the significance threshold.

3.4 H-JADE estimation and causal recovery

We estimate the total-effect matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} using a heteroscedastic-noise-adjusted version of JADE, referred to as H-JADE. The common signal covariance 𝐑s\mathbf{R}_{s} established in Section 3.1 provides the starting point. The observed covariance includes the variant-specific GWAS estimation error, which must be removed before whitening. Write 𝐱jc=𝐱j−𝐱¯\mathbf{x}_{j}^{c}=\mathbf{x}_{j}-\bar{\mathbf{x}} and define

𝐑^s=1N∑j=1N{𝐱jc(𝐱jc)⊤−𝚺jld},𝐇^=𝐑^s−1/2.\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left\{\mathbf{x}_{j}^{c}(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{c})^{\top}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\right\},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{H}}=\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s}^{-1/2}. (3.4)

The whitened observations are 𝐳j=𝐇^​𝐱jc\mathbf{z}_{j}=\widehat{\mathbf{H}}\mathbf{x}_{j}^{c}. To characterise the signal after whitening, let

𝐇=𝐑s−1/2,𝐎=𝐇𝐀𝐃α1/2=(𝐨1,𝐨2),𝐭j=𝐃α−1/2𝐬j.\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{R}_{s}^{-1/2},\qquad\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}=(\mathbf{o}_{1},\mathbf{o}_{2}),\qquad\mathbf{t}_{j}=\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{-1/2}\mathbf{s}_{j}.

Since 𝐑s=𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤\mathbf{R}_{s}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}, 𝐎𝐎⊤=𝐈2\mathbf{O}\mathbf{O}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}_{2}. The signal component after whitening is 𝐲j=𝐎𝐭j\mathbf{y}_{j}=\mathbf{O}\mathbf{t}_{j}, where 𝐎\mathbf{O} is orthogonal and the coordinates of 𝐭j\mathbf{t}_{j} are independent with unit variance. The remaining task is to estimate the orthogonal mixing directions.

LD aggregation also has a tractable effect on the fourth-order information. For a centred variable YY with a finite fourth moment, write cum4⁡(Y)=𝔼⁡(Y4)−3​{𝔼⁡(Y2)}2\operatorname{cum}_{4}(Y)=\mathbb{E}(Y^{4})-3\{\mathbb{E}(Y^{2})\}^{2}. For k=1,2k=1,2, let κα,k=cum4⁡(αj​k)\kappa_{\alpha,k}=\operatorname{cum}_{4}(\alpha_{jk}) denote the fourth-order cumulant of a primitive direct effect, and define

aj,N=∑r=1NRj​r4(∑r=1NRj​r2)2,aN=1N​∑j=1Naj,N.a_{j,N}=\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{4}}{\left(\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{2}\right)^{2}},\qquad a_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}a_{j,N}. (3.5)

Independence of the direct effects across variants yields

cum4⁡(tj​k)=κα,kσα,k4​aj,N.\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{jk})=\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}\,a_{j,N}. (3.6)

Thus LD-score normalisation makes the source variances common, while LD aggregation changes their fourth-order cumulants. The factor aj,Na_{j,N} is shared by the two coordinates, so the variant-specific fourth-order cumulant matrices differ only by a common scalar factor. This structure also matters for the block-bootstrap argument in Section 4.2.

Since Cov⁡(𝐲j)=𝐈2\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y}_{j})=\mathbf{I}_{2}, the average fourth-order cumulant matrix of the whitened signal component, indexed by a symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M}, is

𝐐N​(𝐌)=1N​∑j=1N𝔼⁡{(𝐲j⊤​𝐌𝐲j)​𝐲j​𝐲j⊤}−tr⁡(𝐌)​𝐈2−2​𝐌.\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\!\left\{(\mathbf{y}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{y}_{j})\mathbf{y}_{j}\mathbf{y}_{j}^{\top}\right\}-\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{M})\mathbf{I}_{2}-2\mathbf{M}.

By independence of the source coordinates and (3.6),

𝐎⊤​𝐐N​(𝐌)​𝐎=aN​diag⁡{κα,kσα,k4​(𝐨k⊤​𝐌𝐨k)}k=12.\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M})\mathbf{O}=a_{N}\operatorname{diag}\!\left\{\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}(\mathbf{o}_{k}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{o}_{k})\right\}_{k=1}^{2}. (3.7)

Thus the same orthogonal matrix 𝐎\mathbf{O} diagonalises 𝐐N​(𝐌)\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M}) for every symmetric 𝐌\mathbf{M}. Since the Gaussian summary-statistic errors are independent of the sources and have zero fourth-order cumulants, the noise-corrected fourth-order cumulant matrices have the same diagonalising directions. The factor aNa_{N} changes the magnitude of the fourth-order contrast, but not these directions. The non-degeneracy condition required for their estimation is given in Section 4.1; the derivation of (3.7) is in Supplementary Section S1.4.

To estimate this family of matrices, the covariance terms in the fourth-order moments must be removed variant by variant. Under the theoretical whitening transformation, the covariance of 𝐇𝐱j\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}_{j} is 𝐈2+𝐇​𝚺jld​𝐇⊤\mathbf{I}_{2}+\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\mathbf{H}^{\top}. Accordingly, define

𝐂^j=𝐈2+𝐇^​𝚺jld​𝐇^⊤.\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{j}=\mathbf{I}_{2}+\widehat{\mathbf{H}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}.

For each symmetric 𝐌\mathbf{M}, the noise-corrected sample cumulant matrix is

𝐐^​(𝐌)=1N​∑j=1N{(𝐳j⊤​𝐌𝐳j)​𝐳j​𝐳j⊤−tr⁡(𝐌​𝐂^j)​𝐂^j−2​𝐂^j​𝐌​𝐂^j}.\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}(\mathbf{M})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left\{(\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{z}_{j})\mathbf{z}_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}-\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{M}\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{j})\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{j}-2\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{j}\mathbf{M}\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{j}\right\}. (3.8)

The subtraction consists of the three covariance pairings in a fourth-order cumulant (the last two coincide for symmetric 𝐌\mathbf{M}). A correction based on the average error covariance would generally be insufficient, since the fourth-order correction involves products of variant-specific covariance matrices.

Choose a finite collection ℳ\mathcal{M} spanning the symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrices. The orthogonal directions are estimated by approximate joint diagonalisation:

𝐕^=arg⁡min⁡∑𝐌∈ℳ𝐕∈𝒪⁡(2)⁡‖off⁡{𝐕⊤​𝐐^​(𝐌)​𝐕}‖F2,\widehat{\mathbf{V}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{O}(2)}\sum_{\mathbf{M}\in\mathcal{M}}\left\|\operatorname{off}\{\mathbf{V}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}(\mathbf{M})\mathbf{V}\}\right\|_{F}^{2}, (3.9)

where 𝒪⁡(2)\mathcal{O}(2) denotes the set of 2×22\times 2 orthogonal matrices, off⁡(⋅)\operatorname{off}(\cdot) sets diagonal entries to zero, and ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} is the Frobenius norm. The total-effect matrix is then estimated, up to ICA column scaling and permutation, by

𝐀^=𝐇^−1​𝐕^.\widehat{\mathbf{A}}=\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}. (3.10)

The two causal effects are recovered from 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}} using the identification result in Section 3.2. We invert the estimated mixing matrix, consider its two row orderings, and normalise each admissible ordering to have unit diagonal. The negatives of the resulting off-diagonal entries give the candidate effects β^12\widehat{\beta}_{12} and β^21\widehat{\beta}_{21}. We select the admissible ordering satisfying |β^12​β^21|<1|\widehat{\beta}_{12}\widehat{\beta}_{21}|<1, as established by the stability argument in Section 3.2.

The estimator uses LD scores and variant-specific noise covariance matrices but does not invert the full LD matrix. For fixed trait dimension, the corrected second- and fourth-order moments require one pass over the variants and the joint diagonalisation is fixed-dimensional. The resulting computational cost is linear in NN.

4 Theoretical properties

We study estimation and inference under local dependence of the LD-score normalised rows. Two departures from standard fourth-order ICA drive the asymptotic analysis. First, heteroscedastic Gaussian noise requires variant-specific correction of the sample second- and fourth-order moments. Second, LD induces dependence between nearby variants, so the limiting covariance is a long-run covariance rather than an i.i.d. variance. The resulting ICA estimator is subsequently mapped to the causal effects through the stability-based recovery rule. Technical details and proofs are given in Supplementary Sections S2 and S3.

4.1 Asymptotic distribution under local LD

Recall that 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}, with Cov⁡(𝐞~j)=𝚺jld\operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}. The following condition controls the moments and short-range dependence of the corrected H-JADE moment contributions.

Assumption 4 (Moment and local-dependence conditions).

For some η>0\eta>0:

  1. (i)
    𝔼∥𝜶j⋅∥8+η<∞,supN≥1max1≤j≤N∥𝚺jld∥op<∞;\mathbb{E}\|\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot}\|^{8+\eta}<\infty,\qquad\sup_{N\geq 1}\max_{1\leq j\leq N}\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty;
  2. (ii)

    ordered by chromosome and physical position, the triangular array {(𝐱j,𝚺jld):1≤j≤N}\{(\mathbf{x}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}):1\leq j\leq N\} is strongly mixing, with coefficients αmix​(h)\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(h) satisfying

    ∑h=1∞αmix​(h)η/(8+η)<∞;\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(h)^{\eta/(8+\eta)}<\infty; (4.1)
  3. (iii)

    the long-run covariance of the finite-dimensional corrected moment vector used by H-JADE converges to a finite matrix 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega}.

The 8+η8+\eta moment condition is matched to the fourth-order estimator: the corresponding moment contributions have a 2+η/42+\eta/4 moment, yielding the exponent in (4.1). Neighbouring LD-weighted source vectors can share primitive genetic effects, but the overlap weakens as their genomic separation increases. For finite-range LD, the signal part is itself finite-range dependent; the mixing assumption also covers any remaining short-range dependence in the summary-statistic errors. Part (iii) specifies the limiting long-run covariance 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega} of the corrected moment contributions, accounting for covariance between variants under local dependence. This matrix enters the asymptotic covariance of the causal-effect estimator through the H-JADE estimation and structural recovery. Supplementary Section S2.1 gives the triangular-array formulation of 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega} and relates the mixing condition to overlap between neighbouring LD-weight vectors.

The H-JADE estimator in Section 3.4 relies on fourth-order cumulants, which may vanish even for non-Gaussian sources. Equations (3.5) and (3.6) show that LD aggregation attenuates the standardised fourth-order cumulants of the direct effects by the factors aj,Na_{j,N}. We therefore impose the following condition to ensure sufficient fourth-order contrast for joint diagonalisation as N→∞N\to\infty.

Assumption 5 (Non-degenerate fourth-order contrast).

At most one of κα,1\kappa_{\alpha,1} and κα,2\kappa_{\alpha,2} is zero, and aN→a>0a_{N}\to a>0 as N→∞N\to\infty.

Under Assumption 5, the fourth-order cumulant matrices in (3.7) have a common diagonaliser that is unique up to signed permutation. Further details are given in Supplementary Section S2.2.

Define 𝜷=(β12,β21)⊤\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_{12},\beta_{21})^{\top} and 𝜷^=(β^12,β^21)⊤\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\widehat{\beta}_{12},\widehat{\beta}_{21})^{\top}. The preceding conditions yield root-NN inference for both directional causal effects.

Theorem 2 (Asymptotic distribution of the causal-effect estimator).

Suppose Assumptions 1- 5 hold. Then, as N→∞N\to\infty,

𝐁^→𝑝𝐁,N​(𝜷^−𝜷)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺β),\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{B},\qquad\sqrt{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\beta}),

where 𝚺β=𝐉β​𝛀​𝐉β⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\beta}=\mathbf{J}_{\beta}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{J}_{\beta}^{\top}, and 𝐉β\mathbf{J}_{\beta} is the Jacobian of the locally oriented H-JADE and causal recovery map.

The discrete causal-ordering step is the main addition to ordinary ICA asymptotics. The H-JADE estimate first converges to one representative of the mixing matrix up to scaling and permutation. Stability separates the correct row ordering from the alternative: when both causal effects are nonzero, the two cycle products are reciprocals; when either effect is zero, the candidate under the swapped ordering is not row-normalisable. The correct branch is therefore selected with probability tending to one, after which inversion and row normalisation are smooth. This also shows explicitly that local LD affects the limiting variance through the long-run covariance 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega}; it does not require inversion of the full LD matrix.

4.2 Chromosome-respecting block-bootstrap inference

Direct estimation of 𝚺β\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\beta} would require estimating the long-run covariance of the corrected moments and propagating it through whitening, joint diagonalisation and causal recovery. We instead use a moving block bootstrap that respects chromosome boundaries (Gonçalves and White,, 2002; Lahiri,, 2003).

The resampling unit is the pair (𝐱j,𝚺jld)(\mathbf{x}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}), so that each transformed association remains attached to the covariance used in its heteroscedastic noise correction. Overlapping blocks are sampled only within chromosomes, and each bootstrap sample repeats the complete H-JADE and causal-recovery procedure. Let 𝜷^∗\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*} denote the resulting estimate and define

𝚺^β,MBB=Var∗⁡[N​(𝜷^∗−𝜷^)],\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\beta,\mathrm{MBB}}=\operatorname{Var}^{*}\left[\sqrt{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)\right],

where Var∗\operatorname{Var}^{*} denotes conditional variance given the observed transformed data.

Proposition 2 (Consistency of bootstrap covariance).

Suppose the conditions of Theorem 2 hold. Let NcN_{c} denote the number of variants on chromosome cc, with N=∑c=1CNcN=\sum_{c=1}^{C}N_{c}. Suppose CC is fixed and, as N→∞N\to\infty, Nc/N→πc∈(0,1)N_{c}/N\to\pi_{c}\in(0,1) for each chromosome, while the block length satisfies lN→∞l_{N}\to\infty and lN=o⁡(N1/2)l_{N}=o(N^{1/2}). Then 𝚺^β,MBB→𝑝𝚺β\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\beta,\mathrm{MBB}}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\beta}.

The bootstrap requires an additional argument because the expected fourth-order cumulant contributions vary across variants. In a generic heterogeneous array, such heterogeneity can introduce an additional bootstrap variance term under block resampling (Gonçalves and White,, 2002). Here, however, the noise-adjusted second-order moment is common across variants, while the population counterpart of the jjth corrected fourth-order cumulant contribution satisfies 𝐐j,N​(𝐌)=aj,N​𝐐0,N​(𝐌)\mathbf{Q}_{j,N}(\mathbf{M})=a_{j,N}\mathbf{Q}_{0,N}(\mathbf{M}), where 𝐐0,N​(𝐌)\mathbf{Q}_{0,N}(\mathbf{M}) is common across variants and aj,N>0a_{j,N}>0 is the LD-induced attenuation factor defined in (3.5). Block resampling may therefore alter the overall fourth-order scale, but not the common joint diagonaliser. Since joint diagonalisation and causal recovery are invariant to this rescaling, this scale fluctuation has no first-order effect on the causal estimator. The remaining block-edge effects are asymptotically negligible under the stated block-length condition. Details are given in Supplementary Section S2.3 and the proof of Proposition 2.

With MM bootstrap replications, the covariance of 𝜷^\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} is estimated by the sample covariance of the bootstrap estimates. We use lN≍N1/3l_{N}\asymp N^{1/3}, the standard order for block-bootstrap variance estimation under short-range dependence (Hall et al.,, 1995).

5 Simulation studies

We evaluate the finite-sample performance of H-JADE in estimating and testing bi-directional causal effects. The primary simulations examine estimation accuracy, interval coverage and directional testing in comparison with existing MR methods. We then compare point estimation and computational cost with LHC-MR (Darrous et al.,, 2021) and assess sensitivity to local dependence among direct genetic effects.

5.1 Primary simulations

We generated summary associations from the model in Section 2, with 𝐁0=(0β12β210)\mathbf{B}_{0}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&\beta_{12}\\ \beta_{21}&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) and |β12​β21|<1|\beta_{12}\beta_{21}|<1. The primitive direct effects were independent across traits and variants and followed the two-component Gaussian mixture

αj​k=(1−Uj​k)​Zj​k(small)+Uj​k​Zj​k(large),Uj​k∼Bernoulli⁡(πlarge),\alpha_{jk}=(1-U_{jk})Z_{jk}^{(\mathrm{small})}+U_{jk}Z_{jk}^{(\mathrm{large})},\qquad U_{jk}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{\mathrm{large}}),

where Zj​k(small)∼ℕ⁡(0,σsmall,k2)Z_{jk}^{(\mathrm{small})}\sim\mathbb{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{small},k}^{2}) and Zj​k(large)∼ℕ⁡(0,σlarge,k2)Z_{jk}^{(\mathrm{large})}\sim\mathbb{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{large},k}^{2}). Variants were partitioned into independent LD blocks with within-block AR(1) correlation. Marginal effects were obtained after LD propagation and causal mixing, and heteroscedastic Gaussian estimation errors were generated from effective sample sizes and information scores. The errors shared the within-block correlation structure of the genotypes.

Table 1 gives the six primary designs. Setting 1 sets one directional effect to zero, allowing us to assess how reverse causation affects inference for that null direction. Settings 2–4 have nonzero causal effects in both directions and vary the strength and heterogeneity of LD. Settings 5–6 weaken the genetic signal and Setting 6 additionally allows many small nonzero direct genetic effects. In the hotspot settings, the block-specific AR(1) parameter was sampled from {0.20,0.40,0.60,0.80}\{0.20,0.40,0.60,0.80\}. Each design used N∈{2000,5000}N\in\{2000,5000\} variants, GWAS sample sizes n1=n2=30000n_{1}=n_{2}=30000 for the two traits, and 200 Monte Carlo replications. H-JADE used all variants and 200 moving-block-bootstrap replications. IVW (Burgess et al.,, 2013), MR-Egger (Bowden et al.,, 2015), the weighted median (Bowden et al.,, 2016), and MR-RAPS (Zhao et al.,, 2020) were fitted separately in each direction after selection at p<10−5p<10^{-5} and LD clumping at r2<0.001r^{2}<0.001. MR-RAPS used over-dispersion with Huber loss. Further implementation details and additional numerical results are given in Supplementary Section S4.

Estimation and interval coverage.

Tables 2 and 3 report the empirical bias and Monte Carlo standard deviation of the estimators, and the empirical coverage probability and average length of nominal 95% confidence intervals, respectively, for N=5000N=5000. Each entry gives the first measure followed by the second in parentheses. The corresponding results for N=2000N=2000 are provided in Supplementary Section S4.1.

H-JADE estimates were approximately centred across the primary designs. At N=5000N=5000, the largest absolute bias was 0.007, and the Monte Carlo standard deviation was smaller than at N=2000N=2000 in every setting and direction. In contrast, the direction-specific estimators showed substantial bias in several feedback settings. For example, when β12=−0.4\beta_{12}=-0.4 in Setting 3, IVW and MR-RAPS had positive mean estimates, while the H-JADE mean was −0.405-0.405. MR-Egger was more variable in several settings, particularly under weaker genetic signals. H-JADE also maintained relatively stable empirical coverage across the primary settings, whereas IVW, MR-RAPS and the weighted median frequently showed substantial undercoverage. MR-Egger generally produced considerably wider confidence intervals.

Directional testing.

We compared H-JADE with the directional focusing procedures of Li and Ye, (2025). Their method forms a direction-specific focused set using strong exposure associations and small standardised outcome associations under the directional null, and then applies IVW or median inference. We used focused IVW (Fo-IVW) with focusing threshold τf=1.2\tau_{f}=1.2 or 1.5 and focused median (Fo-Median) with τf=1.5\tau_{f}=1.5, following the released implementation; a smaller τf\tau_{f} gives a more selective focused set. H-JADE rejected a directional null when the corresponding 95% confidence interval based on moving-block-bootstrap standard errors excluded zero.

Setting 1 has a null 2→12\to 1 effect. To examine the other orientation, we also interchanged the zero and nonzero effects, setting (β12,β21)=(0.5,0)(\beta_{12},\beta_{21})=(0.5,0). H-JADE rejection probabilities for the two null directions were 0.090 and 0.070 at N=2000N=2000, and 0.070 and 0.055 at N=5000N=5000. The three focusing procedures ranged from 0.010 to 0.055 over these four null cases. Figure 1 reports the empirical rejection rates for the nonzero setting–direction combinations. H-JADE had the highest rejection rate in all 11 setting–direction combinations at both NN. The complete results are given in Supplementary Section S4.2.

5.2 Comparison with LHC-MR

We also compared point estimation with LHC-MR (Darrous et al.,, 2021), which jointly estimates the two causal directions under a parametric model for the genetic architecture and uses multi-start likelihood optimisation for estimation. We considered two scenarios. In the first, the two primitive source processes were independent, making it compatible with the working structures of both methods. In the second, we introduced the shared heritable component modelled by LHC-MR, inducing dependence between the two source processes and thereby violating the InDiE condition used by H-JADE.

Five independent data sets were generated in each scenario, with 5000 input variants and (β12,β21)=(−0.4,0.5)(\beta_{12},\beta_{21})=(-0.4,0.5). LHC-MR used 50 likelihood starts and its preprocessing retained 500 variants. H-JADE was fitted both to this same 500-variant panel and to all 5000 variants. Table 4 reports descriptive means, root mean squared errors (RMSEs) and point-estimation times. Across the five data sets in the independent-source scenario, LHC-MR had smaller RMSE than H-JADE on the matched panel, while full-panel H-JADE had the smallest RMSE in both directions. In the shared-heritable-component scenario, departures from the generating values were mainly in the β12\beta_{12} direction and were most pronounced for LHC-MR. Estimates of β21\beta_{21} remained close to the true value for all three fits. The computational difference was substantial: median LHC-MR point-estimation time was about 7.9 hours per data set on our computing platform, compared with less than 0.5 seconds for full-panel H-JADE. These timings cover point estimation only; they exclude H-JADE moving-block-bootstrap inference and LHC-MR block-jackknife inference. Individual estimates and further implementation details are given in Supplementary Section S4.3.

5.3 Sensitivity to local dependence

The primary simulations assume that the primitive direct effects are independent across variants. To assess sensitivity to this condition, we introduced short-range dependence within each trait-specific direct-effect sequence while retaining independence between the two sequences. Using Setting 6, the direct genetic effects within each LD block were generated from normalised MA(5) processes, with θk\theta_{k} controlling the strength of local dependence for trait kk. We considered (θ1,θ2)∈{(0,0),(0.2,0.5),(0.5,0.5),(0.8,0.5)}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in\{(0,0),(0.2,0.5),(0.5,0.5),(0.8,0.5)\}. The values θ=0.5\theta=0.5 and 0.8 correspond to lag-one correlations of about 0.50 and 0.77, respectively, and (θ1,θ2)=(0,0)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=(0,0) reproduces Setting 6 replication by replication.

Table 5 reports the results at N=5000N=5000. Empirical biases remained small across all dependence settings. For β^12\widehat{\beta}_{12}, the Monte Carlo standard deviation varied across settings, while the ratio of the average bootstrap standard error to the Monte Carlo standard deviation declined from 0.968 to 0.855, with empirical coverage decreasing from 0.960 to 0.905. For β^21\widehat{\beta}_{21}, the variation in Monte Carlo standard deviation and empirical coverage was smaller, although the corresponding SE/SD ratio also declined from 0.974 to 0.936.

Under MA(5) dependence, the covariance of the LD-score-normalised source vectors varies across variants. However, the two trait-specific source processes remain independent, so their average covariance is diagonal and whitening based on the average signal covariance retains an orthogonal mixing structure. The MA construction introduces additional dependence between neighbouring variants beyond that induced by LD aggregation, altering the cross-variant covariance of the corrected moment contributions. These features are consistent with the small empirical biases and the changes in Monte Carlo standard deviations and bootstrap standard errors observed in the simulations. Further diagnostics are given in Supplementary Section S4.4.

6 Real-data analysis

We analysed three cardiometabolic trait pairs: low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)–coronary heart disease (CHD), apolipoprotein B (ApoB)–CHD, and triglycerides (TG)–type 2 diabetes (T2D). GWAS summary statistics were obtained through the MRC IEU OpenGWAS infrastructure (Hemani et al.,, 2018; Elsworth et al.,, 2020). Dataset identifiers and original GWAS sources are listed in Supplementary Table S7. For each pair, the two GWAS were conducted in distinct studies using European-ancestry samples. All GWAS associations and standard errors were converted to the standardised-genotype scale. Lipid associations remain on standardised phenotype scales, whereas CHD and T2D associations remain on log-odds scales. Causal estimates involving binary disease exposures therefore require cautious interpretation (Burgess and Labrecque,, 2018).

After allele harmonisation, H-JADE used the common harmonised variant panel for the two traits together with a European-ancestry LD-score reference (Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015a, ; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015b, ). Standard errors were obtained from 200 moving block bootstrap replications. The four direction-specific estimators used in Section 5—IVW, MR-Egger, MR-RAPS and the weighted median—were fitted separately after exposure-specific selection and LD clumping. We also applied the Fo-IVW and Fo-Median directional tests with the same tuning values as in Section 5.1. Further implementation details and complete results are in Supplementary Section S5.

Figure 2 shows the point estimates from the five methods and their 95% confidence intervals. Table 6 reports the pp-values from H-JADE and the directional focusing tests for each causal direction.

For LDL-C–CHD, all five estimators supported a positive LDL-C-to-CHD effect, consistent with established genetic evidence (Richardson et al.,, 2020). The reverse direction showed greater disagreement: H-JADE estimated a significant negative effect (−0.0257-0.0257, SE 0.00910.0091), consistent in sign with the weighted median, whereas IVW gave a significant positive estimate and none of the focusing tests rejected the null. Previous reverse-MR evidence also suggested that greater coronary disease liability may be associated with lower LDL-C, potentially reflecting lipid-lowering treatment (Smith et al.,, 2023).

For ApoB–CHD, all five estimators again supported a positive forward effect, consistent with the established importance of ApoB in coronary risk (Zuber et al.,, 2021). However, despite using the same CHD GWAS, the reverse results differed from those for LDL-C: H-JADE estimated an effect close to zero (−0.0003-0.0003, SE 0.01070.0107), and none of the focusing tests rejected the null, whereas IVW and the weighted median yielded significant estimates with opposite signs. These two applications highlight the method sensitivity of reverse inference even for closely related lipid traits.

For TG–T2D, the most notable disagreement arose in the TG-to-T2D direction: IVW, MR-RAPS and the weighted median, together with all three focusing tests, detected a positive effect, whereas H-JADE did not reject the null (0.0740.074, SE 0.1330.133). The latter finding is consistent with an earlier MR study reporting no evidence that genetically elevated TG increases T2D risk (de Silva et al.,, 2011). In the reverse direction, H-JADE detected a positive T2D-to-TG effect (0.0880.088, SE 0.0130.013), supported by IVW, MR-RAPS and the weighted median but only one of the three focusing tests. This direction is also consistent with genetic evidence linking diabetes liability and glycaemic traits to elevated TG (Smith et al.,, 2023; Zhu et al.,, 2022).

Across the three applications, H-JADE agreed with direction-specific methods in several well-established directions but yielded different conclusions for CHD-to-LDL-C, CHD-to-ApoB and TG-to-T2D. These contrasts illustrate how conclusions may change when the two causal directions are modelled jointly rather than analysed separately using direction-specific instruments.

7 Discussion and conclusion

This article introduces a novel method for bi-directional Mendelian randomization by linking it to independent component analysis: LD-score-normalised GWAS associations can be expressed as noisy linear mixtures of LD-aggregated direct genetic effects. Under the InDiE condition, informative non-Gaussianity of the direct genetic effects identifies the total-effect matrix up to the usual ICA ambiguities, while the no-self-feedback and stability restrictions recover the two directional causal effects. Identification therefore comes from the distributional structure of direct genetic effects rather than from valid instrumental variables.

A key challenge in using the InDiE condition for bi-directional MR is that, unlike unidirectional MR, selecting variants based on marginal associations can induce dependence between the two latent source components, thereby violating the independence assumption underlying ICA. Estimation from GWAS summary statistics additionally requires accounting for variant-specific estimation errors and LD. To address these, we use LD-score normalisation to avoid inverting the full LD matrix. The H-JADE algorithm developed here has computational complexity linear in the number of genetic variants. LD-induced local dependence is accounted for in the asymptotic covariance, and inference is based on a moving block bootstrap that respects chromosome boundaries. In the primary simulations, H-JADE produced accurate point estimates and generally satisfactory confidence interval coverage. It also achieved higher power for nonzero directional effects than the focusing procedures of Li and Ye, (2025), with significantly shorter computation times than LHC-MR (Darrous et al.,, 2021). The real-data analyses show that joint estimation of the feedback system can lead to different conclusions from separate unidirectional MR analyses.

A natural extension is to feedback systems involving more than two traits. The noisy-ICA representation extends directly, but structural recovery becomes more difficult: the two-trait problem reduces to choosing between two orderings, whereas higher-dimensional systems admit many possible permutations and feedback structures. Developing recovery rules that resolve this ambiguity is an important direction for future work.

Data availability

GWAS summary statistics used in the real-data analyses were obtained from IEU OpenGWAS (Elsworth et al.,, 2020). The corresponding GWAS IDs are listed in Supplementary Table S7. The R code implementing the proposed method and used for the simulation studies and real-data analyses is available at https://github.com/molly3687/bidirectional-mr-hjade/tree/main/R.

Supplementary Material for
Identification and Inference of Bi-directional Causal Effects in Mendelian Randomization without Instrument Selection

Liyuan Mo*, Qingyuan Zhao†,‡\dagger,\ddagger

This supplement provides technical details for the noisy independent component analysis formulation and asymptotic theory, complete proofs of the theoretical results, additional simulation results and diagnostics, and further information for the real-data applications.

S1 Technical details for the noisy ICA formulation

This section provides technical details for the noisy ICA representation used in Section 3. It compares the model with ordinary ICA, expands the interpretation of the direct-effect assumption and the effect of variant selection, establishes an ICA identification result, and derives the noise-adjusted second- and fourth-order quantities used to estimate the total-effect matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}.

S1.1 Relation to ordinary ICA

For a single observation, ordinary ICA is usually written as 𝐱=𝐀𝐬\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}, where the coordinates of 𝐬\mathbf{s} are mutually independent and the observations are often treated as independent and identically distributed. The model used in this paper is different in three ways.

First, the observations are not individual-level phenotypes. They are variant-level pairs of marginal GWAS association estimates after LD-score normalisation:

𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j,j=1,…,N.\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,N. (S1.1)

The mixing matrix 𝐀=(𝐈2−𝐁)−1\mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1} is the total-effect matrix of the bi-directional trait system.

Second, the latent sources are not the original direct genetic effects 𝜶j⋅\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot}. They are LD-weighted effective sources, 𝐬j=ℓj−1/2∑r=1NRj​r𝜶r⋅\mathbf{s}_{j}=\ell_{j}^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{r\cdot}. Thus the sequence {𝐬j:1≤j≤N}\{\mathbf{s}_{j}:1\leq j\leq N\} is generally dependent along the genome, even when the direct effects {𝜶j⋅:1≤j≤N}\{\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot}:1\leq j\leq N\} are independent across variants.

Third, the additive error is heteroscedastic: Cov⁡(𝐞~j)=ℓj−1​𝚺j\operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j})=\ell_{j}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}. Consequently, whitening based on the observed covariance does not generally yield an orthogonal signal mixing matrix, and conventional fourth-order sample cumulants do not directly recover the corresponding signal cumulants. Both the whitening step and the fourth-order cumulant step must therefore be corrected for the variant-specific error covariance.

The LD-score transformation is used to stabilise the scale of the latent source, not to make the variants independent. Indeed,

Var⁡(sj​k)=ℓj−1​∑r=1NRj​r2​σα,k2=σα,k2,\operatorname{Var}(s_{jk})=\ell_{j}^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{2}\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{2}=\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{2},

but nearby 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j}’s may still be dependent because their LD windows overlap. The dependence affects large-sample variance and bootstrap inference, but it does not by itself affect identification of the common mixing matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}. The following result gives the ICA part of the identification argument.

Theorem S1 (ICA identifiability of the total-effect matrix).

Consider the LD-score transformed model 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}. Suppose Assumptions 2 and 3 hold and 𝐀\mathbf{A} is invertible. Then 𝐀\mathbf{A} is identifiable from the distribution of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} up to column scaling and permutation.

For later use, define the row-normalisation map for a matrix with nonzero diagonal entries by

𝒩⁡(𝐌~)={diag⁡(M~11,M~22)}−1​𝐌~.\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}})=\{\operatorname{diag}(\widetilde{M}_{11},\widetilde{M}_{22})\}^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}. (S1.2)

If 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}} is an ICA mixing-matrix estimate, let 𝐏π\mathbf{P}_{\pi} denote either of the two candidate row-permutation matrices. The corresponding demixing candidate is

𝐖^​(𝐏π)=𝒩⁡(𝐏π​𝐀^−1),\widehat{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{P}_{\pi})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{-1}\right), (S1.3)

provided that both diagonal entries of 𝐏π​𝐀^−1\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{-1} are nonzero; otherwise that ordering is inadmissible.

The following proposition gives the two-trait form of the stability-based causal recovery argument for cyclic structural models (Lacerda et al.,, 2008).

Proposition S1 (Causal recovery from the total-effect matrix).

Suppose |β12​β21|<1|\beta_{12}\beta_{21}|<1, 𝐀=(𝐈2−𝐁)−1\mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}, and ICA identifies 𝐀\mathbf{A} up to column scaling and permutation. Then 𝐁\mathbf{B} is uniquely recovered by inverting the identified mixing matrix, normalising the admissible row orderings to have unit diagonal, and retaining the stable ordering.

Theorem S1 therefore identifies 𝐀\mathbf{A} up to scaling and permutation. These remaining indeterminacies are resolved by the cyclic MR structure in Section 3.2.

S1.2 Source assumptions and variant selection

Assumption 3 is imposed on the primitive direct genetic effects 𝜶j⋅\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j\cdot}, before LD aggregation and causal feedback, rather than on the observed marginal associations. Independence across primitive variants is therefore compatible with dependence among nearby rows of 𝐑​𝜶\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\alpha}. The identical-distribution condition posits a common marginal distribution for the variant-level direct genetic effects and is compatible with polygenic architectures having many small effects and a smaller fraction of larger effects (Zhou et al.,, 2013; Moser et al.,, 2015; Boyle et al.,, 2017).

The cross-trait condition αj​1⟂⟂αj​2\alpha_{j1}\perp\!\!\!\perp\alpha_{j2} rules out systematic alignment of the two direct-effect architectures before causal propagation. It does not require a variant to act directly on only one trait: both components may be nonzero for the same variant. The condition is related to independence restrictions that separate instrument strength from direct effects in robust MR, but it is imposed on the latent direct genetic effects across the common harmonised variant panel rather than on a selected instrument set (Bowden et al.,, 2015; Bowden,, 2017; Wu et al.,, 2025). Non-Gaussianity supplies the distributional information required for ICA identification (Comon,, 1994; Hyvärinen and Oja,, 2000) and is compatible with sparse, heavy-tailed and mixture effect distributions (Zhou et al.,, 2013; Moser et al.,, 2015; Boyle et al.,, 2017).

Proposition 1 in the main paper shows that selection on mixed marginal associations generally truncates the source distribution over a non-product region and thereby changes its independence structure. For noisy GWAS summary statistics, write 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j} and let ℰj={𝐱j∈𝒞}\mathcal{E}_{j}=\{\mathbf{x}_{j}\in\mathcal{C}\}. Define the selection probability conditional on the latent source by

qj​(𝐬)=ℙ⁡(𝐀𝐬+𝐞~j∈𝒞∣𝐬j=𝐬).q_{j}(\mathbf{s})=\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}\in\mathcal{C}\mid\mathbf{s}_{j}=\mathbf{s}\right).

The conditional law of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} given selection is proportional to qj​(𝐬)q_{j}(\mathbf{s}) times its original product law. Source independence is therefore preserved only when this weight factorises, up to a multiplicative constant, into separate functions of the two source coordinates. The noise-free result is the special case qj(𝐬)=𝟏{𝐬∈𝐀−1𝒞}q_{j}(\mathbf{s})=\mathbf{1}\{\mathbf{s}\in\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathcal{C}\}.

Selection mechanisms independent of the marginal associations, or regions that are separable in the latent source coordinates, preserve the product structure. Direction-specific significance selection on mixed marginal associations generally does not. This structural effect is distinct from winner’s curse, post-selection bias, loss of polygenic signal and sensitivity to significance or LD-clumping thresholds (Wang and Han,, 2021; Ma et al.,, 2023; Jiang et al.,, 2023; Zhao et al.,, 2019). The proof of Proposition 1 is given in Section S3.2.

S1.3 Noise-adjusted whitening

For the transformed model 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}, recall that 𝐃α=Cov⁡(𝐬j)\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}=\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{s}_{j}), with 𝐃α=diag⁡(σα,12,σα,22)\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{\alpha,1}^{2},\sigma_{\alpha,2}^{2}). The signal covariance is 𝐑s=𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤\mathbf{R}_{s}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}. The observed covariance contains the additional contribution of the summary-statistic error. Since this contribution varies with jj, we estimate the signal covariance by

𝐑^s=1N​∑j=1N{𝐱jc​(𝐱jc)⊤−𝚺jld},𝚺jld=ℓj−1​𝚺j.\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left\{\mathbf{x}_{j}^{c}(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{c})^{\top}-{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\,\mathrm{ld}}_{j}\right\},\qquad{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\,\mathrm{ld}}_{j}=\ell_{j}^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}.

Let 𝐇^=𝐑^s−1/2\widehat{\mathbf{H}}=\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s}^{-1/2} be the estimated whitening matrix. With 𝐇=𝐑s−1/2\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{R}_{s}^{-1/2}, we have 𝐎=𝐇𝐀𝐃α1/2∈𝒪⁡(2)\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}\in\mathcal{O}(2), because

𝐎𝐎⊤=𝐇𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤​𝐇⊤=𝐈2.\mathbf{O}\mathbf{O}^{\top}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{H}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}_{2}.

Thus whitening reduces the estimation of 𝐀\mathbf{A} to the estimation of an orthogonal rotation 𝐎\mathbf{O}, followed by the inverse whitening map.

𝐇𝐱j=𝐎𝐭j+𝜻j,𝐭j=𝐃α−1/2𝐬j,𝜻j=𝐇𝐞~j.\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{O}\mathbf{t}_{j}+\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j},\qquad\mathbf{t}_{j}=\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{-1/2}\mathbf{s}_{j},\qquad\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j}=\mathbf{H}\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}.

We now derive the cumulant identity underlying the common-diagonaliser representation in (3.7) of the main paper. For k=1,2k=1,2, write κ¯k,N=N−1​∑j=1Ncum4⁡(tj​k)\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{jk}). By component-wise independence of tj​1t_{j1} and tj​2t_{j2}, the corrected fourth-order cumulant matrix satisfies

Consequently, pre- and postmultiplying (S1.5) by 𝐎⊤\mathbf{O}^{\top} and 𝐎\mathbf{O} yields (3.7) of the main paper. In particular, the same 𝐎\mathbf{O} jointly diagonalises these matrices for every symmetric 𝐌\mathbf{M}. For estimation, choose a finite collection ℳ={𝐌1,…,𝐌L}\mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{M}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{M}_{L}\} spanning the space of symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrices. Compute 𝐐^ℓ=𝐐^(𝐌ℓ),ℓ=1,…,L\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}=\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}(\mathbf{M}_{\ell}),\quad\ell=1,\ldots,L, and estimate the orthogonal rotation by

𝐕^=arg⁡min⁡∑ℓ=1L𝐕∈𝒪⁡(2)⁡‖off⁡(𝐕⊤​𝐐^ℓ​𝐕)‖F2.\widehat{\mathbf{V}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{O}(2)}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left\|\operatorname{off}\left(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}\mathbf{V}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}.

The estimated mixing matrix is then 𝐀^=𝐇^−1​𝐕^\widehat{\mathbf{A}}=\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}. The orientation of 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}} remains subject to column scaling and column permutation, as in ordinary ICA. These ambiguities are handled using the causal structure in Section 3.2.

S1.5 Fourth-order contrast and weak dependence

Theorem S1 establishes ICA identification under component-wise independence and the usual non-Gaussianity condition. The H-JADE estimator, however, uses fourth-order cumulants. We therefore need fourth-order contrast for the cumulant-based implementation.

A sufficient condition is that κ¯k,N→κk\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}\to\kappa_{k} for k=1,2k=1,2 as N→∞N\to\infty, where κ1\kappa_{1} and κ2\kappa_{2} are not both zero. A formal version of this condition is given in Assumption 5. Under this condition, the family of matrices in (S1.5) contains enough fourth-order information to identify the orthogonal rotation 𝐎\mathbf{O} up to the usual signed permutation. This condition is the fourth-order analogue of the non-Gaussianity requirement in ordinary ICA.

Weak dependence along the genome does not change the diagonal form in (S1.5). It affects the stochastic convergence of the estimated matrices 𝐐^​(𝐌)\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}(\mathbf{M}) and the covariance of the resulting estimator.

S2 Additional details for the asymptotic theory

This section gives the technical details behind the asymptotic results in Section 4 of the main paper. We first describe the corrected moment vector and its long-run covariance under local LD, then record the fourth-order contrast after LD aggregation, and finally give the chromosome-respecting moving block bootstrap construction. Complete proofs follow in Section S3. Unless otherwise specified, asymptotic statements in this section and the proofs are for N→∞N\to\infty, with the number of traits fixed.

S2.1 Moment conditions and local LD

Assumption 4 is stated for the primitive direct effects because they are the independent genetic inputs in the structural model. For p=8+ηp=8+\eta, write wj​r=Rj​r/ℓj1/2w_{jr}=R_{jr}/\ell_{j}^{1/2}, so that ∑r=1Nwj​r2=1\sum_{r=1}^{N}w_{jr}^{2}=1. Standard moment inequalities for weighted sums of independent, mean-zero vectors then give supj𝔼​‖𝐬j‖8+η<∞\sup_{j}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{s}_{j}\|^{8+\eta}<\infty. The uniform operator-norm bound on 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}} similarly bounds every Gaussian error moment needed in the second- and fourth-order corrections. Hence 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j} has uniformly bounded 8+η8+\eta moments.

The raw sample contributions entering the corrected moment vector are polynomials of degree at most four in 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}, with coefficients depending on 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}. They have uniformly bounded 2+δ2+\delta moments with δ=η/4\delta=\eta/4, and the standard covariance inequality for strongly mixing sequences therefore uses δ2+δ=η8+η\frac{\delta}{2+\delta}=\frac{\eta}{8+\eta}, which explains the exponent in (4.1). The assumption is a high-level representation of local LD rather than an independence condition. A useful measure of overlap between two LD-weighted source vectors is

ω⁡(h)=supj∑r=1N|Rj​r​Rj+h,r|ℓj1/2​ℓj+h1/2.\omega(h)=\sup_{j}\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{N}|R_{jr}R_{j+h,r}|}{\ell_{j}^{1/2}\ell_{j+h}^{1/2}}.

Decay of ω⁡(h)\omega(h) with genomic distance motivates the mixing condition. In the idealized case Rj​r=0R_{jr}=0 whenever |j−r|>m|j-r|>m, the transformed sequence is 2​m2m-dependent, apart from chromosome boundaries, and the summability condition holds automatically.

For the proofs below, let 𝝁^N\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N} denote the finite-dimensional vector of corrected second- and fourth-order sample moments used by H-JADE, let 𝝁N\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N} be its population counterpart, and let 𝐦j,N\mathbf{m}_{j,N} denote the corresponding centred first-order contribution from variant jj. The long-run covariance is

𝛀N=1N​∑i=1N∑j=1NCov⁡(𝐦i,N,𝐦j,N)⟶𝛀.\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{m}_{i,N},\mathbf{m}_{j,N})\longrightarrow\boldsymbol{\Omega}. (S2.1)

It retains covariance terms between nearby variants and reduces to a sum of marginal variances only under independence.

Let {uj,N:1≤j≤N}\{u_{j,N}:1\leq j\leq N\} be a mean-zero scalar triangular array. Suppose that, for some δ>0\delta>0,

1mN​∑j∈INuj,N→𝑑ℕ⁡(0,v).\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_{N}}}\sum_{j\in I_{N}}u_{j,N}\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}(0,v).

Moreover, for every deterministic sequence mN→∞m_{N}\to\infty with mN≤Nm_{N}\leq N,

limM→∞lim supN→∞supI⊆[N]​ contiguous|I|=mN𝔼[(∑j∈Iuj,N)2mN{(∑j∈Iuj,N)2mN>M}]=0.\lim_{M\to\infty}\limsup_{N\to\infty}\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subseteq[N]\text{ contiguous}\\ |I|=m_{N}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{(\sum_{j\in I}u_{j,N})^{2}}{m_{N}}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{\frac{(\sum_{j\in I}u_{j,N})^{2}}{m_{N}}>M\right\}\right]=0. (S2.2)
