Under Assumptions 2, 3, and 4,

N​(𝝁^N−𝝁N)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝛀).\sqrt{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega}).

S2.2 Fourth-order contrast under LD aggregation

Let tj​k=sj​k/σα,kt_{jk}=s_{jk}/\sigma_{\alpha,k}. Independence of the primitive direct effects across variants gives

cum4⁡(tj​k)=κα,kσα,k4​∑r=1NRj​r4(∑r=1NRj​r2)2.\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{jk})=\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{4}}{\left(\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{2}\right)^{2}}.

Accordingly, let 𝐐j,N​(𝐌)\mathbf{Q}_{j,N}(\mathbf{M}) denote the theoretical noise-adjusted fourth-order cumulant contribution of variant jj. Then

𝐐j,N​(𝐌)=𝐎​diag​{(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)11​cum4⁡(tj​1),(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)22​cum4⁡(tj​2)}​𝐎⊤=aj,N​𝐐0,N​(𝐌),\mathbf{Q}_{j,N}(\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{O}\operatorname{diag}\!\left\{(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{11}\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{j1}),(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{22}\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{j2})\right\}\mathbf{O}^{\top}=a_{j,N}\mathbf{Q}_{0,N}(\mathbf{M}),

where

𝐐0,N​(𝐌)=𝐎​diag⁡{(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)11​κα,1σα,14,(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)22​κα,2σα,24}​𝐎⊤.\mathbf{Q}_{0,N}(\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{O}\operatorname{diag}\!\left\{(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{11}\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,1}}{\sigma_{\alpha,1}^{4}},(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{22}\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,2}}{\sigma_{\alpha,2}^{4}}\right\}\mathbf{O}^{\top}.

Averaging over variants yields

κ¯k,N=1N​∑j=1Ncum4⁡(tj​k)=κα,kσα,k4​aN⟶κα,kσα,k4​a.\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{jk})=\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}a_{N}\longrightarrow\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}a.

Thus, when a>0a>0, LD aggregation attenuates but does not asymptotically eliminate any primitive fourth-order contrast for which κα,k≠0\kappa_{\alpha,k}\neq 0. As shown in Section S1.4, the noise-adjusted fourth-order cumulant matrices 𝐐N​(𝐌)\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M}) in (S1.5) admit representations of the form

𝐐N​(𝐌)=𝐎​diag⁡{(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)11​κ¯1,N,(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)22​κ¯2,N}​𝐎⊤,\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{O}\operatorname{diag}\left\{(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{11}\bar{\kappa}_{1,N},(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{22}\bar{\kappa}_{2,N}\right\}\mathbf{O}^{\top},

and all the matrices 𝐐N​(𝐌)\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M}) can be jointly diagonalized by the same orthogonal matrix 𝐎\mathbf{O}. Under Assumption 5, at most one source direction has a vanishing fourth-order contrast. The joint diagonalization therefore identifies 𝐎\mathbf{O} uniquely up to signed permutation.

Assumption 5 therefore combines a primitive fourth-cumulant condition with a requirement that LD aggregation not wash out the contrast asymptotically. This is a condition for the fourth-order H-JADE implementation, not for general independent-component identification. A non-Gaussian distribution may have zero fourth cumulant and remain identifiable through another contrast, while providing no identifying information to a method based only on fourth-order cumulants.

Proposition S2 (Local asymptotic distribution of the H-JADE mixing estimate).

Under the conditions of Theorem 2, fix a local signed-permutation branch of the joint diagonaliser. Let 𝐀^loc\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}} be the corresponding locally oriented representative of the H-JADE mixing estimate. There exist a permutation matrix 𝐏0\mathbf{P}_{0} and a nonsingular diagonal matrix 𝚲0\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0} such that, with 𝐀0=𝐀𝐏0​𝚲0\mathbf{A}_{0}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0},

𝐀^loc→𝑝𝐀0,N​vec⁡(𝐀^loc−𝐀0)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺A),\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{A}_{0},\qquad\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{A}_{0})\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}),

where 𝚺A=𝐉A​𝛀​𝐉A⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}=\mathbf{J}_{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{J}_{A}^{\top} and 𝐉A\mathbf{J}_{A} is the Jacobian of the locally oriented H-JADE map.

S2.3 Chromosome-respecting moving block bootstrap

Let 𝒟N={(𝐱j,𝚺jld):j=1,…,N}\mathcal{D}_{N}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}):j=1,\ldots,N\}, with variants ordered by chromosome and physical position. The transformed association and its variant-specific noise covariance are resampled together, so every bootstrap observation retains the covariance used in the heteroscedastic Gaussian-noise correction.

Suppose chromosome cc contributes NcN_{c} variants. For a global block length lNl_{N}, set lN,c=min⁡(lN,Nc)l_{N,c}=\min(l_{N},N_{c}). The overlapping blocks on chromosome cc are

ℬc,r={(𝐱c,r+k,𝚺c,r+kld):0≤k≤lN,c−1},r=1,…,Nc−lN,c+1.\mathcal{B}_{c,r}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{c,r+k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c,r+k}^{\mathrm{ld}}):0\leq k\leq l_{N,c}-1\},\qquad r=1,\ldots,N_{c}-l_{N,c}+1.

Blocks are sampled independently with replacement within each chromosome until exactly NcN_{c} bootstrap observations have been generated; the last sampled block is truncated if necessary. The chromosome-specific samples are then concatenated. Hence every bootstrap data set contains exactly NN observation–covariance pairs and preserves the original number of variants on each chromosome. Under Proposition 2, Nc/N→πc>0N_{c}/N\to\pi_{c}>0 and lN=o⁡(N1/2)l_{N}=o(N^{1/2}), so lN,c=lNl_{N,c}=l_{N} for all chromosomes for sufficiently large NN.

Each bootstrap sample repeats centring, covariance correction, whitening, corrected cumulant construction, joint diagonalisation, structural normalisation and stability-based ordering. The implementation uses lN=round⁡(3​N1/3)l_{N}=\operatorname{round}(3N^{1/3}) and M=200M=200 bootstrap replications in the reported analyses.

The proposition concerns the ideal conditional covariance. For the full causal matrix, write

𝚺^B,MBB=Var∗⁡[N​vec⁡(𝐁^∗)].\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{B,\mathrm{MBB}}=\operatorname{Var}^{*}\!\left[\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{*})\right].

If 𝐄β\mathbf{E}_{\beta} extracts the two off-diagonal entries from vec⁡(𝐁)\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{B}), then 𝚺β=𝐄β​𝚺B​𝐄β⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\beta}=\mathbf{E}_{\beta}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B}\mathbf{E}_{\beta}^{\top}, and the covariance in Proposition 2 is the corresponding projection of 𝚺^B,MBB\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{B,\mathrm{MBB}}. With MM Monte Carlo replications, let 𝐛^∗(m)=vec⁡(𝐁^∗(m))\widehat{\mathbf{b}}^{*(m)}=\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{*(m)}) and 𝐛¯∗=M−1​∑m=1M𝐛^∗(m)\overline{\mathbf{b}}^{*}=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\widehat{\mathbf{b}}^{*(m)}. The sample covariance

𝐕^B,M=1M−1​∑m=1M(𝐛^∗(m)−𝐛¯∗)​(𝐛^∗(m)−𝐛¯∗)⊤\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{B,M}=\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\widehat{\mathbf{b}}^{*(m)}-\overline{\mathbf{b}}^{*})(\widehat{\mathbf{b}}^{*(m)}-\overline{\mathbf{b}}^{*})^{\top} (S2.3)

is the Monte Carlo approximation to the conditional covariance of vec⁡(𝐁^∗)\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{*}); equivalently, N​𝐕^B,MN\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{B,M} approximates 𝚺^B,MBB\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{B,\mathrm{MBB}}, which is the ideal bootstrap covariance studied in Proposition 2.

The centred first-order moment array has a uniformly bounded 2+η/42+\eta/4 moment and satisfies the same mixing summability condition as in Assumption 4. The proof of Proposition 2 shows directly that these conditions give the required conditional covariance and second-moment tail control.

The remaining issue is variation in the expected fourth-order cumulant contributions across variants. The expected noise-adjusted second-order moment is constant across variants, whereas

𝐐j,N​(𝐌)=aj,N​𝐐0,N​(𝐌),aj,N=∑r=1NRj​r4(∑r=1NRj​r2)2.\mathbf{Q}_{j,N}(\mathbf{M})=a_{j,N}\mathbf{Q}_{0,N}(\mathbf{M}),\qquad a_{j,N}=\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{4}}{(\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{2})^{2}}.

Because each bootstrap sample has exactly NN observations, bootstrap reweighting replaces aN=N−1​∑jaj,Na_{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{j}a_{j,N} by a weighted average of the same positive aj,Na_{j,N}’s. Thus, the fourth-order cumulant matrices are all rescaled by one common positive factor. Joint diagonalisation and causal recovery are exactly invariant to this common rescaling, including the change in weights caused by truncating the final block. The proof consequently expands only the centred bootstrap fluctuation around this scale-invariant path of theoretical moments.

The ideal bootstrap map uses a uniformly bounded extension of the locally identified H-JADE and causal-recovery map outside a fixed regular neighbourhood. It agrees with the stated estimator on that neighbourhood. The proof shows that the complement has conditional probability op​(N−1)o_{p}(N^{-1}) and makes an asymptotically negligible contribution to the root-NN second moment.

S3 Proofs of the theoretical results

This section contains the proofs of the theoretical results in the main paper and this supplement.

S3.1 Proof of Theorem S1

Proof.

The argument concerns identifiability from the observed distribution. It does not require the sequence {𝐬j}j=1N\{\mathbf{s}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} to be independent or identically distributed across jj. Dependence between effective source vectors corresponding to nearby variants is therefore irrelevant for the present result. The proof uses only the marginal distribution at a fixed index jj, the non-Gaussianity and within-index independence of the two source components, and the fact that the same mixing matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} is shared across all variants.

Fix j∈[N]j\in[N]. Recall that 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}, where 𝐞~j∼ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺jld)\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}\sim\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\right) is independent of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j}. Since 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}} is known as part of the summary-statistic error model, the Gaussian noise distribution is known. The characteristic function of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} is therefore

φ𝐱j​(𝐭)=φ𝐀𝐬j​(𝐭)​exp⁡{−12​𝐭⊤​𝚺jld​𝐭},𝐭∈ℝ2.\varphi_{\mathbf{x}_{j}}(\mathbf{t})=\varphi_{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}}(\mathbf{t})\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\mathbf{t}\right\},\qquad\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. (S3.1)

The Gaussian characteristic function is strictly positive for every 𝐭\mathbf{t}. Consequently, the characteristic function of the signal part is uniquely determined by the distribution of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}:

φ𝐀𝐬j​(𝐭)=φ𝐱j​(𝐭)​exp⁡{12​𝐭⊤​𝚺jld​𝐭}.\varphi_{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}}(\mathbf{t})=\varphi_{\mathbf{x}_{j}}(\mathbf{t})\exp\left\{\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\mathbf{t}\right\}. (S3.2)

Thus the distribution of 𝐀𝐬j\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j} is identified by Gaussian deconvolution. In particular, the additive Gaussian noise introduces no additional ambiguity in the identification of the signal distribution.

We next verify that the effective source vector 𝐬j=(sj​1,sj​2)⊤\mathbf{s}_{j}=(s_{j1},s_{j2})^{\top} satisfies the standard ICA non-Gaussianity condition. From the LD-score transformation, sj​k=ℓj−1/2∑r=1NRj​rαr​ks_{jk}=\ell_{j}^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}\alpha_{rk} for k=1,2k=1,2. The two components sj​1s_{j1} and sj​2s_{j2} are mutually independent because they are measurable functions of the two mutually independent families {αr​1:r∈[N]}and{αr​2:r∈[N]}\{\alpha_{r1}:r\in[N]\}\quad\text{and}\quad\{\alpha_{r2}:r\in[N]\}, respectively.

Moreover, at most one of sj​1s_{j1} and sj​2s_{j2} is Gaussian. To see this, suppose that sj​ks_{jk} is Gaussian for some kk. It is a finite sum of independent random variables. By Cramér’s decomposition theorem, every non-degenerate summand ℓj−1/2Rj​rαr​k\ell_{j}^{-1/2}R_{jr}\alpha_{rk} with Rj​r≠0R_{jr}\neq 0 must then be Gaussian. Since Rj​j=1R_{jj}=1, the coefficient of αj​k\alpha_{jk} in this sum is nonzero. Hence αj​k\alpha_{jk} must be Gaussian. Assumption 3 allows at most one of the two primitive component distributions to be Gaussian. It follows that at most one component of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} is Gaussian.

Now suppose that the same marginal distribution of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} admits another representation in the same model class:

𝐱j=d𝐀⋆​𝐬j⋆+𝐞~j⋆,\mathbf{x}_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\mathbf{A}^{\star}\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}^{\star}, (S3.3)

where 𝐀⋆\mathbf{A}^{\star} is nonsingular, 𝐞~j⋆∼ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺jld)\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}^{\star}\sim\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\right) is independent of 𝐬j⋆\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star}, and the two components of 𝐬j⋆\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star} are mutually independent, non-degenerate, and contain at most one Gaussian component.

Applying the same Gaussian deconvolution as in (S3.2) to the two representations gives 𝐀𝐬j=d𝐀⋆​𝐬j⋆\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\mathbf{A}^{\star}\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star}. Since 𝐀\mathbf{A} is nonsingular under the stability condition, define 𝐂=𝐀−1​𝐀⋆\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A}^{\star}. Then

𝐬j=d𝐂𝐬j⋆.\mathbf{s}_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star}. (S3.4)

Because the components of 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} are independent, the two components of 𝐂𝐬j⋆\mathbf{C}\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star} are also independent.

Write

𝐂=(C11C12C21C22),\mathbf{C}=\begin{pmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\ C_{21}&C_{22}\end{pmatrix},

and define the two linear forms

L1=C11​sj​1⋆+C12​sj​2⋆,L2=C21​sj​1⋆+C22​sj​2⋆.L_{1}=C_{11}s_{j1}^{\star}+C_{12}s_{j2}^{\star},\qquad L_{2}=C_{21}s_{j1}^{\star}+C_{22}s_{j2}^{\star}.

By (S3.4), L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} are independent. The Darmois–Skitovich theorem (Darmois,, 1953; Skitovich,, 1953) therefore implies that any source component sj​k⋆s_{jk}^{\star} whose coefficients are nonzero in both L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} must be Gaussian.

First suppose that both components of 𝐬j⋆\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\star} are non-Gaussian. Then neither source component can appear in both linear forms. Consequently, each column of 𝐂\mathbf{C} contains at most one nonzero entry. Since 𝐂\mathbf{C} is nonsingular, every column and every row must contain exactly one nonzero entry.

It remains to consider the case in which exactly one source component is Gaussian. Without loss of generality, suppose that sj​2⋆s_{j2}^{\star} is Gaussian and sj​1⋆s_{j1}^{\star} is non-Gaussian. The Darmois–Skitovich theorem (Darmois,, 1953; Skitovich,, 1953) implies C11​C21=0C_{11}C_{21}=0, because the non-Gaussian component sj​1⋆s_{j1}^{\star} cannot enter both L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}.

Suppose, for example, that C11≠0,C21=0C_{11}\neq 0,\quad C_{21}=0. Nonsingularity of 𝐂\mathbf{C} then implies C22≠0C_{22}\neq 0. Since L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} are independent and have finite second moments,

0=Cov⁡(L1,L2)=C12​C22​Var⁡(sj​2⋆),\displaystyle 0=\operatorname{Cov}(L_{1},L_{2})=C_{12}C_{22}\operatorname{Var}(s_{j2}^{\star}),

where the cross-covariance involving sj​1⋆s_{j1}^{\star} vanishes by source independence. Since C22≠0C_{22}\neq 0 and Var⁡(sj​2⋆)>0\operatorname{Var}(s_{j2}^{\star})>0, it follows that C12=0C_{12}=0. Hence 𝐂\mathbf{C} has exactly one nonzero entry in every row and column. The case C11=0,C21≠0C_{11}=0,\quad C_{21}\neq 0 is symmetric. Therefore the same conclusion holds when one source component is Gaussian.

We have shown in all cases that 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a generalized permutation matrix. Hence there exist a permutation matrix 𝐏\mathbf{P} and a nonsingular diagonal matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D} such that 𝐂=𝐏𝐃\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}. It follows that 𝐀⋆=𝐀𝐂=𝐀𝐏𝐃\mathbf{A}^{\star}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}.

Therefore the mixing matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} is identified from the marginal distribution of the LD-score-transformed summary statistics up to column permutation and nonsingular column scaling.

The argument was carried out at a fixed variant index jj. It does not require the sequence {𝐬j}j=1N\{\mathbf{s}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} to be independent or identically distributed across variants. Cross-variant dependence induced by LD affects estimation and inference, but not identification of the common mixing matrix. ∎

Proof.

d​νjd​μj​(u,v)=𝟏𝒟​(u,v)pj,μj​-almost everywhere.\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu_{j}}{\mathrm{d}\mu_{j}}(u,v)=\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{D}}(u,v)}{p_{j}},\qquad\mu_{j}\text{-almost everywhere}.

Define B1={u∈ℝ:hj​1​(u)>0},B2={v∈ℝ:hj​2​(v)>0}B_{1}=\{u\in\mathbb{R}:h_{j1}(u)>0\},\quad B_{2}=\{v\in\mathbb{R}:h_{j2}(v)>0\}. Because pj>0p_{j}>0, the preceding equality implies

for μj\mu_{j}-almost every (u,v)(u,v). Therefore, μj​(𝒟△(B1×B2))=0\mu_{j}\!\left(\mathcal{D}\mathbin{\triangle}(B_{1}\times B_{2})\right)=0, where △\triangle denotes symmetric difference. Equivalently, 𝐀−1​𝒞=B1×B2\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathcal{C}=B_{1}\times B_{2} up to a μj\mu_{j}-null set.

S3.3 Proof of Proposition S1

Proof.

Let

𝐖=𝐀−1=𝐈2−𝐁=(1−β12−β211).\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\beta_{12}\\ -\beta_{21}&1\end{pmatrix}.

𝐖ICA:=(𝐀ICA)−1=𝐃−1​𝐏⊤​𝐖.\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ICA}}:=(\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{ICA}})^{-1}=\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{W}.

Thus 𝐖ICA\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ICA}} differs from the structural demixing matrix 𝐖\mathbf{W} only by row scaling and row permutation.

Let 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} denote the set of 2×22\times 2 permutation matrices. Here 𝐏\mathbf{P} is the column permutation in the ICA representation, whereas 𝐏π\mathbf{P}_{\pi} indexes a candidate row ordering of the demixing matrix. For each 𝐏π∈𝒫2\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}, define 𝐖~​(𝐏π)=𝐏π​𝐖ICA\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{P}_{\pi})=\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{ICA}}. Consider first the row permutation 𝐏π=𝐏\mathbf{P}_{\pi}=\mathbf{P}. Then 𝐖~​(𝐏)=𝐏𝐃−1​𝐏⊤​𝐖\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{P})=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{W}. The matrix 𝚲:=𝐏𝐃−1​𝐏⊤\boldsymbol{\Lambda}:=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{P}^{\top} is nonsingular and diagonal. Because the diagonal entries of 𝐖\mathbf{W} are equal to one, the normalisation is well defined, and 𝐖⁡(𝐏)=𝒩⁡(𝚲​𝐖)=𝐖\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{P})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{W})=\mathbf{W}. Consequently, 𝐁⁡(𝐏)=𝐈2−𝐖=𝐁\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{P})=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{B}. This candidate satisfies the stability condition |β12​β21|<1|\beta_{12}\beta_{21}|<1.

It remains to examine the only other row permutation. Let

𝐉=(0110)\mathbf{J}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}

denote the swap matrix. Since 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} contains exactly two elements, the alternative row permutation is 𝐏π=𝐉𝐏\mathbf{P}_{\pi}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}. For this permutation,

𝐖~​(𝐉𝐏)=𝐉​𝚲​𝐖=(𝐉​𝚲​𝐉)​(𝐉𝐖).\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P})=\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{W}=(\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{J})(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}).

Because 𝐉​𝚲​𝐉\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{J} is again a nonsingular diagonal matrix, row normalisation removes this factor whenever the normalisation is well defined. Hence 𝐖⁡(𝐉𝐏)=𝒩⁡(𝐉𝐖)\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}). Now

𝐉𝐖=(−β2111−β12).\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}=\begin{pmatrix}-\beta_{21}&1\\ 1&-\beta_{12}\end{pmatrix}.

If β12​β21=0\beta_{12}\beta_{21}=0, then at least one diagonal entry of 𝐉𝐖\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W} is zero. The row normalisation 𝒩⁡(𝐉𝐖)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}) is therefore not well defined, so the row-swapped candidate is inadmissible.

Suppose instead that β12​β21≠0\beta_{12}\beta_{21}\neq 0. Row normalisation then gives

𝐖⁡(𝐉𝐏)=(1−1/β21−1/β121),\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P})=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1/\beta_{21}\\ -1/\beta_{12}&1\end{pmatrix},

Thus the swapped candidate violates the stability condition.

Thus, if β12​β21=0\beta_{12}\beta_{21}=0, the swapped candidate cannot be row-normalised, while if β12​β21≠0\beta_{12}\beta_{21}\neq 0, it yields an unstable causal matrix. In either case, the correctly ordered candidate is the unique admissible stable candidate. Since this candidate satisfies 𝐁⁡(𝐏)=𝐁\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{P})=\mathbf{B}, the causal matrix 𝐁\mathbf{B} is uniquely recovered. ∎

S3.4 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

Theorem S1 identifies the total-effect matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} up to the usual ICA scaling and permutation ambiguities. Proposition S1 resolves these ambiguities under the no-self-feedback constraint and stability condition, and hence uniquely recovers 𝐁\mathbf{B}. The conclusion follows. ∎

S3.6 Proof of Lemma S2

Proof.

Throughout the proof, the dependence of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}, 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j}, and 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}} on NN is suppressed in the notation. Let δ=η4\delta=\frac{\eta}{4}. Then 2+δ=2+η/42+\delta=2+\eta/4 and δ/(2+δ)=η/(8+η)\delta/(2+\delta)=\eta/(8+\eta).

We first express the sample H-JADE moments as a function of a finite-dimensional vector of raw sample moments. Because ℳ\mathcal{M} is finite and the dimension of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} is fixed at two, there exists a finite-dimensional measurable map 𝝍:ℝ2×ℝ2×2⟶ℝd\boldsymbol{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} such that 𝐫j,N=𝝍⁡(𝐱j,𝚺jld)\mathbf{r}_{j,N}=\boldsymbol{\psi}\left(\mathbf{x}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\right) collects all raw quantities required to construct the entries of 𝝁^N\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}. In particular, it is sufficient for 𝐫j,N\mathbf{r}_{j,N} to contain the monomials in the entries of 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} of orders one through four, together with the entries of 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}} and their second-order products. Define

𝜽^N=1N​∑j=1N𝐫j,N,𝜽N=1N​∑j=1N𝔼⁡(𝐫j,N).\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{r}_{j,N},\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{r}_{j,N}).

Centering, noise-covariance subtraction, inverse-square-root whitening, and the corrected cumulant construction are finite-dimensional smooth operations whenever the signal covariance is positive definite. Consequently, there is a map 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi}, continuously twice differentiable on a neighborhood of 𝜽N\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}, such that 𝝁^N=𝚽⁡(𝜽^N)\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}) and 𝝁N=𝚽⁡(𝜽N)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}). Indeed, the centring identities express all sample central moments of order at most four as polynomials in the corresponding raw moments. Moreover, the signal covariance is 𝐑s=𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤\mathbf{R}_{s}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}. Since 𝐀\mathbf{A} is nonsingular and 𝐃α\mathbf{D}_{\alpha} is positive definite under Assumption 3, 𝐑s\mathbf{R}_{s} is positive definite. The inverse-square-root map is therefore smooth in a neighborhood of 𝐑s\mathbf{R}_{s}. Because ℳ\mathcal{M} is finite, the derivatives of 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} are uniformly bounded on a sufficiently small neighborhood of 𝜽N\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}.

We next establish the required moment bounds. Set p=8+ηp=8+\eta. For wj​r=Rj​rℓj1/2w_{jr}=\frac{R_{jr}}{\ell_{j}^{1/2}}, we have ∑r=1Nwj​r2=1\sum_{r=1}^{N}w_{jr}^{2}=1. Since p>2p>2, it also follows that ∑r=1N|wj​r|p≤∑r=1Nwj​r2=1\sum_{r=1}^{N}|w_{jr}|^{p}\leq\sum_{r=1}^{N}w_{jr}^{2}=1. Applying the standard moment inequality for weighted sums of independent mean-zero random vectors to 𝐬j=∑r=1Nwj​r𝜶r⋅\mathbf{s}_{j}=\sum_{r=1}^{N}w_{jr}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{r\cdot} and using Assumption 4(i) gives

supN≥1maxj∈[N]⁡𝔼​‖𝐬j‖8+η<∞.\sup_{N\geq 1}\max_{j\in[N]}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{s}_{j}\|^{8+\eta}<\infty.

Under Assumption 2, the transformed error 𝐞~j\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j} is Gaussian with covariance 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}. The uniform boundedness of 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}} therefore implies

supN≥1maxj∈[N]⁡𝔼​‖𝐞~j‖8+η<∞.\sup_{N\geq 1}\max_{j\in[N]}\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}\|^{8+\eta}<\infty.

Since 𝐱j=𝐀𝐬j+𝐞~j\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_{j}+\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}, we consequently obtain

supN≥1maxj∈[N]⁡𝔼​‖𝐱j‖8+η<∞.\sup_{N\geq 1}\max_{j\in[N]}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{x}_{j}\|^{8+\eta}<\infty. (S3.8)

Every coordinate of 𝐫j,N\mathbf{r}_{j,N} is a polynomial of degree at most four in 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}, with coefficients involving bounded functions of 𝚺jld\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}. Because 4​(2+δ)=4​(2+η4)=8+η4(2+\delta)=4\left(2+\frac{\eta}{4}\right)=8+\eta, equation (S3.8) implies

supN≥1maxj∈[N]⁡𝔼​‖𝐫j,N‖2+δ<∞.\sup_{N\geq 1}\max_{j\in[N]}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{r}_{j,N}\|^{2+\delta}<\infty. (S3.9)

The array {𝐫j,N:j∈[N]}\left\{\mathbf{r}_{j,N}:j\in[N]\right\} is strongly mixing with coefficients bounded by αmix​(h)\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(h), because 𝐫j,N\mathbf{r}_{j,N} is a measurable function of (𝐱j,𝚺jld)(\mathbf{x}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}). For each coordinate a∈[d]a\in[d], set Yj,N(a)=rj,N(a)−𝔼⁡(rj,N(a))Y_{j,N}^{(a)}=r_{j,N}^{(a)}-\mathbb{E}\bigl(r_{j,N}^{(a)}\bigr). Davydov’s covariance inequality and (S3.9) give a constant C<∞C<\infty, independent of i,ji,j, and NN, such that

|Cov⁡(Yi,N(a),Yj,N(a))|≤C​αmix​(|i−j|)δ/(2+δ)=C​αmix​(|i−j|)η/(8+η).\left|\operatorname{Cov}\left(Y_{i,N}^{(a)},Y_{j,N}^{(a)}\right)\right|\leq C\,\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(|i-j|)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}=C\,\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(|i-j|)^{\eta/(8+\eta)}.

It follows that

Var⁡(1N​∑j=1NYj,N(a))\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{j,N}^{(a)}\right) ≤CN2​∑i=1N∑j=1Nαmix​(|i−j|)η/(8+η)\displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{N^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(|i-j|)^{\eta/(8+\eta)}
≤CN​{1+2​∑h=1N−1αmix​(h)η/(8+η)}.\displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{N}\left\{1+2\sum_{h=1}^{N-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(h)^{\eta/(8+\eta)}\right\}.

By (4.1), the expression in braces is uniformly bounded. Hence 𝜽^N−𝜽N=Op(N−1/2)\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}).

Let 𝐆N=D​𝚽​(𝜽N)\mathbf{G}_{N}=D\boldsymbol{\Phi}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}\right) be the Jacobian of 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} at 𝜽N\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}. A second-order Taylor expansion gives

𝝁^N−𝝁N\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N} =𝐆N​(𝜽^N−𝜽N)+𝐑N,\displaystyle=\mathbf{G}_{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}\right)+\mathbf{R}_{N}, (S3.10)

where

∥𝐑N∥=Op(∥𝜽^N−𝜽N∥2)=Op(N−1)=op(N−1/2).\|\mathbf{R}_{N}\|=O_{p}\left(\|\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}\|^{2}\right)=O_{p}(N^{-1})=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}).

The centred first-order contribution of variant jj is

𝐦j,N=𝐆N​{𝐫j,N−𝔼⁡(𝐫j,N)}.\mathbf{m}_{j,N}=\mathbf{G}_{N}\left\{\mathbf{r}_{j,N}-\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{r}_{j,N})\right\}.

Then 𝔼⁡(𝐦j,N)=𝟎\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{m}_{j,N})=\mathbf{0} and

𝐆N​(𝜽^N−𝜽N)=1N​∑j=1N𝐦j,N.\mathbf{G}_{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}\right)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{j,N}.

Thus (S3.10) becomes

𝝁^N−𝝁N=1N∑j=1N𝐦j,N+op(N−1/2).\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{j,N}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). (S3.11)

Since the matrices 𝐆N\mathbf{G}_{N} are uniformly bounded, (S3.9) also gives uniformly bounded (2+δ)(2+\delta)-th moments for 𝐦j,N\mathbf{m}_{j,N}. The same covariance argument as above consequently gives 1N∑j=1N𝐦j,N=Op(N−1/2)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{j,N}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}). Together with (S3.11), this proves 𝝁^N−𝝁N=op​(1)\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}=o_{p}(1).

It remains to establish asymptotic normality. Fix 𝐭∈ℝq\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}, and define Uj,N​(𝐭)=𝐭⊤​𝐦j,NU_{j,N}(\mathbf{t})=\mathbf{t}^{\top}\mathbf{m}_{j,N}. The scalar triangular array {Uj,N​(𝐭):j∈[N]}\{U_{j,N}(\mathbf{t}):j\in[N]\} is strongly mixing with coefficients bounded by αmix​(h)\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(h), and

supN≥1maxj∈[N]⁡𝔼​|Uj,N​(𝐭)|2+δ<∞.\sup_{N\geq 1}\max_{j\in[N]}\mathbb{E}|U_{j,N}(\mathbf{t})|^{2+\delta}<\infty.

Moreover, by (S2.1),

1N​Var⁡{∑j=1NUj,N​(𝐭)}\displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\operatorname{Var}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{N}U_{j,N}(\mathbf{t})\right\} =𝐭⊤​𝛀N​𝐭⟶𝐭⊤​𝛀​𝐭.\displaystyle=\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{N}\mathbf{t}\longrightarrow\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{t}.

Lemma S1, applied to the full interval IN=[N]I_{N}=[N], therefore gives

1N​∑j=1NUj,N​(𝐭)→𝑑ℕ⁡(0,𝐭⊤​𝛀​𝐭).\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}U_{j,N}(\mathbf{t})\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(0,\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{t}\right).

Therefore, for every fixed 𝐭∈ℝq\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},

𝐭⊤​1N​∑j=1N𝐦j,N→𝑑ℕ⁡(0,𝐭⊤​𝛀​𝐭).\mathbf{t}^{\top}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{j,N}\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(0,\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{t}\right).

The Cramér–Wold device now yields

1N​∑j=1N𝐦j,N→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝛀).\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{j,N}\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega}\right).

Finally, multiplying (S3.11) by N\sqrt{N} and applying Slutsky’s theorem gives

N​(𝝁^N−𝝁N)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝛀).\sqrt{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega}\right).

This completes the proof. ∎

S3.7 Proof of Proposition S2

Proof.

Let 𝐃α=diag⁡(σα,12,σα,22)\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{\alpha,1}^{2},\sigma_{\alpha,2}^{2}). By Assumption 3, 𝐃α\mathbf{D}_{\alpha} is positive definite. Besides, 𝐀=(𝐈2−𝐁)−1\mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B})^{-1} is nonsingular. Hence the signal covariance 𝐑s=𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤\mathbf{R}_{s}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top} is positive definite. Define 𝐇=𝐑s−1/2\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{R}_{s}^{-1/2} and 𝐎=𝐇𝐀𝐃α1/2\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}. Then

𝐎𝐎⊤\displaystyle\mathbf{O}\mathbf{O}^{\top} =𝐇𝐀𝐃α​𝐀⊤​𝐇⊤\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{H}^{\top}
=𝐇𝐑s​𝐇⊤=𝐈2,\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{R}_{s}\mathbf{H}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}_{2},

so that 𝐎∈𝒪⁡(2)\mathbf{O}\in\mathcal{O}(2).

Writing 𝐭j=𝐃α−1/2𝐬j\mathbf{t}_{j}=\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{-1/2}\mathbf{s}_{j}, applying the theoretical whitening matrix gives

𝐇𝐱j=𝐎𝐭j+𝜻j,𝜻j=𝐇​𝐞~j.\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathbf{O}\mathbf{t}_{j}+\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j},\qquad\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j}=\mathbf{H}\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{j}.

The components of 𝐭j\mathbf{t}_{j} are mutually independent and have unit variance. The covariance matrix of 𝜻j\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{j} is 𝐕j=𝐇​𝚺jld​𝐇⊤\mathbf{V}_{j}=\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{\mathrm{ld}}\mathbf{H}^{\top}. For k=1,2k=1,2, define

κ¯k,N=1N​∑j=1Ncum4⁡(tj​k).\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{jk}).

Because

tj​k=1σα,k​ℓj1/2​∑r=1NRj​r​αr​k,t_{jk}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}\ell_{j}^{1/2}}\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}\alpha_{rk},

the independence of the primitive effects across rr gives

cum4⁡(tj​k)=κα,kσα,k4​∑r=1NRj​r4(∑r=1NRj​r2)2.\operatorname{cum}_{4}(t_{jk})=\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{4}}{\left(\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}^{2}\right)^{2}}.

Consequently,

κ¯k,N=κα,kσα,k4​aN⟶κk:=κα,kσα,k4​a.\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}=\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}a_{N}\longrightarrow\kappa_{k}:=\frac{\kappa_{\alpha,k}}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{4}}a.

By Assumption 5, at most one of κ1\kappa_{1} and κ2\kappa_{2} is zero.

For every symmetric 𝐌∈ℝ2×2\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, the population counterpart of the corrected cumulant matrix in (S1.4) is, by (S1.5),

𝐐N​(𝐌)=𝐎​diag⁡{(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)11​κ¯1,N,(𝐎⊤​𝐌𝐎)22​κ¯2,N}​𝐎⊤.\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{O}\operatorname{diag}\left\{(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{11}\bar{\kappa}_{1,N},\,(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{O})_{22}\bar{\kappa}_{2,N}\right\}\mathbf{O}^{\top}.

The subscript NN is retained here because the averaged effective-source cumulants depend on NN.

Let ℳ={𝐌1,…,𝐌L}\mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{M}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{M}_{L}\} span the space of symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrices, and define 𝐐ℓ,N=𝐐N(𝐌ℓ),ℓ=1,…,L\mathbf{Q}_{\ell,N}=\mathbf{Q}_{N}(\mathbf{M}_{\ell}),\quad\ell=1,\ldots,L. Then 𝐎⊤​𝐐ℓ,N​𝐎=𝐃ℓ,N\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{\ell,N}\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{D}_{\ell,N}, where 𝐃ℓ,N=diag⁡(dℓ​1,N,dℓ​2,N)\mathbf{D}_{\ell,N}=\operatorname{diag}\left(d_{\ell 1,N},d_{\ell 2,N}\right) and dℓ​k,N=κ¯k,N​(𝐎⊤​𝐌ℓ​𝐎)k​kd_{\ell k,N}=\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{\ell}\mathbf{O})_{kk}.

Define the joint-diagonalization separation quantity

ΔN=∑ℓ=1L(dℓ​1,N−dℓ​2,N)2.\Delta_{N}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left(d_{\ell 1,N}-d_{\ell 2,N}\right)^{2}.

We claim that

lim infN→∞ΔN>0.\liminf_{N\to\infty}\Delta_{N}>0. (S3.12)

To verify this, let dℓ​k=κk​(𝐎⊤​𝐌ℓ​𝐎)k​kd_{\ell k}=\kappa_{k}(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{\ell}\mathbf{O})_{kk} and Δ=∑ℓ=1L(dℓ​1−dℓ​2)2\Delta=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(d_{\ell 1}-d_{\ell 2})^{2}. Since κ¯k,N→κk\bar{\kappa}_{k,N}\to\kappa_{k}, we have ΔN→Δ\Delta_{N}\to\Delta.

Suppose that Δ=0\Delta=0. Then, for every ℓ\ell,

κ1​(𝐎⊤​𝐌ℓ​𝐎)11=κ2​(𝐎⊤​𝐌ℓ​𝐎)22.\kappa_{1}(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{\ell}\mathbf{O})_{11}=\kappa_{2}(\mathbf{O}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{\ell}\mathbf{O})_{22}.

Because ℳ\mathcal{M} spans the symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrices, the same identity holds for every symmetric matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M}. Taking 𝐌=𝐎𝐞1​𝐞1⊤​𝐎⊤\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{O}\mathbf{e}_{1}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{O}^{\top} gives κ1=0\kappa_{1}=0, whereas taking 𝐌=𝐎𝐞2​𝐞2⊤​𝐎⊤\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{O}\mathbf{e}_{2}\mathbf{e}_{2}^{\top}\mathbf{O}^{\top} gives κ2=0\kappa_{2}=0. This contradicts Assumption 5. Therefore Δ>0\Delta>0, proving (S3.12).

We next derive the stochastic behaviour of the whitening step. The entries of 𝐑^s\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s} form part of the estimated moment vector 𝝁^N\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}. Lemma S2 therefore implies 𝐑^s−𝐑s=Op(N−1/2)\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s}-\mathbf{R}_{s}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}). Since 𝐑s\mathbf{R}_{s} is positive definite, ℙ{λmin(𝐑^s)>0}⟶1\mathbb{P}\left\{\lambda_{\min}(\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s})>0\right\}\longrightarrow 1.

Both matrix maps 𝐑⟼𝐑−1/2\mathbf{R}\longmapsto\mathbf{R}^{-1/2}and 𝐑⟼𝐑1/2\mathbf{R}\longmapsto\mathbf{R}^{1/2} are continuously Fréchet differentiable on the cone of positive-definite matrices. Hence 𝐇^−𝐇=Op(N−1/2)\widehat{\mathbf{H}}-\mathbf{H}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}) and 𝐇^−1−𝐇−1=Op(N−1/2)\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}). More precisely, since 𝐑^s\widehat{\mathbf{R}}_{s} is a coordinate of 𝝁^N\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}, there exists a matrix 𝐉H−1\mathbf{J}_{H^{-1}} such that

vec(𝐇^−1−𝐇−1)=𝐉H−1(𝝁^N−𝝁N)+op(N−1/2).\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right)=\mathbf{J}_{H^{-1}}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}\right)+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). (S3.13)

Consequently, N​vec⁡(𝐇^−1−𝐇−1)\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right) is asymptotically normal.

We now consider the orthogonal joint-diagonalization step. Define the population and empirical criteria

ℒN​(𝐕)=∑ℓ=1L‖off⁡(𝐕⊤​𝐐ℓ,N​𝐕)‖F2\mathcal{L}_{N}(\mathbf{V})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left\|\operatorname{off}\left(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{\ell,N}\mathbf{V}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}

and

ℒ^N​(𝐕)=∑ℓ=1L‖off⁡(𝐕⊤​𝐐^ℓ​𝐕)‖F2.\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{N}(\mathbf{V})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left\|\operatorname{off}\left(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}\mathbf{V}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}.

Because the entries of the corrected cumulant matrices are included in 𝝁^N\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}, Lemma S2 gives

max1≤ℓ≤L‖𝐐^ℓ−𝐐ℓ,N‖F=Op(N−1/2).\max_{1\leq\ell\leq L}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}-\mathbf{Q}_{\ell,N}\right\|_{F}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}).

Since LL is fixed and 𝒪⁡(2)\mathcal{O}(2) is compact,

sup𝐕∈𝒪⁡(2)|ℒ^N​(𝐕)−ℒN​(𝐕)|=op​(1).\sup_{\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{O}(2)}\left|\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{N}(\mathbf{V})-\mathcal{L}_{N}(\mathbf{V})\right|=o_{p}(1).

By (S3.12), the population minimisers of ℒN\mathcal{L}_{N}, for all sufficiently large NN, are precisely 𝐎𝐒\mathbf{O}\mathbf{S}, where 𝐒\mathbf{S} ranges over the 2×22\times 2 signed permutation matrices. Thus the orthogonal rotation is identified up to the usual sign and permutation indeterminacies.

Fix one local signed-permutation branch and choose its representative 𝐕0=𝐎𝐒0\mathbf{V}_{0}=\mathbf{O}\mathbf{S}_{0}. Since the signed-permutation orbit is finite, uniform convergence and (S3.12) allow a signed-permutation matrix 𝐒N\mathbf{S}_{N} to be chosen so that the locally oriented estimator

𝐕^loc:=𝐕^​𝐒N→𝑝𝐕0.\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}:=\widehat{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{S}_{N}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{V}_{0}.

The subsequent local expansion concerns this representative, not an arbitrary orientation returned by the joint-diagonalisation algorithm.

We next verify the local nonsingularity needed for the root-NN expansion. Let

𝐑⁡(ϑ)=(cos⁡ϑ−sin⁡ϑsin⁡ϑcos⁡ϑ)\mathbf{R}(\vartheta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\vartheta&-\sin\vartheta\\ \sin\vartheta&\cos\vartheta\end{pmatrix}

and use the local parameterization 𝐕⁡(ϑ)=𝐕0​𝐑​(ϑ)\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)=\mathbf{V}_{0}\mathbf{R}(\vartheta). After the fixed signed permutation has been absorbed into the diagonal entries, write

𝐕0⊤​𝐐ℓ,N​𝐕0=diag⁡(dℓ​1,N(0),dℓ​2,N(0)).\mathbf{V}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{\ell,N}\mathbf{V}_{0}=\operatorname{diag}(d_{\ell 1,N}^{(0)},d_{\ell 2,N}^{(0)}).

The corresponding theoretical criterion is

ℒN​{𝐕⁡(ϑ)}\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{N}\{\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)\} =2​∑ℓ=1L(dℓ​1,N(0)−dℓ​2,N(0))2​sin2⁡ϑ​cos2⁡ϑ\displaystyle=2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left(d_{\ell 1,N}^{(0)}-d_{\ell 2,N}^{(0)}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}\vartheta\cos^{2}\vartheta
=2​ΔN​sin2⁡ϑ​cos2⁡ϑ.\displaystyle=2\Delta_{N}\sin^{2}\vartheta\cos^{2}\vartheta.

Therefore,

∂∂ϑ​ℒN​{𝐕⁡(ϑ)}|ϑ=0=0\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\vartheta}\mathcal{L}_{N}\{\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)\}\right|_{\vartheta=0}=0

and

∂2∂ϑ2​ℒN​{𝐕⁡(ϑ)}|ϑ=0=4​ΔN.\left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\vartheta^{2}}\mathcal{L}_{N}\{\mathbf{V}(\vartheta)\}\right|_{\vartheta=0}=4\Delta_{N}. (S3.14)

By (S3.12), the quantity in (S3.14) is bounded away from zero for all sufficiently large NN.

The first-order condition for the sample criterion at the locally oriented minimiser is

∂∂ϑ​ℒ^N​{𝐕0​𝐑​(ϑ)}|ϑ=ϑ^N=0.\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\vartheta}\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{N}\{\mathbf{V}_{0}\mathbf{R}(\vartheta)\}\right|_{\vartheta=\widehat{\vartheta}_{N}}=0.

The score is a continuously differentiable function of the entries of the corrected cumulant matrices. The nonsingularity in (S3.14) therefore permits application of the implicit function theorem. It follows that the locally oriented joint diagonalizer is a continuously differentiable function of the estimated moment vector in a neighborhood of 𝝁N\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}. Consequently, for some matrix 𝐉V\mathbf{J}_{V},

vec(𝐕^loc−𝐕0)=𝐉V(𝝁^N−𝝁N)+op(N−1/2).\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{V}_{0}\right)=\mathbf{J}_{V}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}\right)+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). (S3.15)

In particular, 𝐕^loc−𝐕0=Op(N−1/2)\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{V}_{0}=O_{p}(N^{-1/2}), and Lemma S2 gives the asymptotic normality of the locally oriented 𝐕^loc\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}. This is the two-dimensional local joint-diagonalization perturbation argument underlying the general results for fourth-order ICA estimators.

We now combine the whitening and rotation steps. By (3.10) and the definition of the local orientation, 𝐀^loc=𝐇^−1​𝐕^loc\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}=\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}. Its target under the chosen local orientation is

𝐀0:=𝐇−1​𝐕0=𝐇−1​𝐎𝐒0=𝐀𝐃α1/2​𝐒0.\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{0}:=\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{V}_{0}=\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{O}\mathbf{S}_{0}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}\mathbf{S}_{0}.

Write the signed permutation matrix as 𝐒0=𝐏0​𝐃0\mathbf{S}_{0}=\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{D}_{0}, where 𝐏0\mathbf{P}_{0} is a permutation matrix and 𝐃0\mathbf{D}_{0} is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries in {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. Then

𝐃α1/2​𝐒0=𝐃α1/2​𝐏0​𝐃0=𝐏0​(𝐏0⊤​𝐃α1/2​𝐏0)​𝐃0.\displaystyle\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}\mathbf{S}_{0}=\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{D}_{0}=\mathbf{P}_{0}\left(\mathbf{P}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}\mathbf{P}_{0}\right)\mathbf{D}_{0}.

Hence, with

𝚲0=(𝐏0⊤​𝐃α1/2​𝐏0)​𝐃0,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}=\left(\mathbf{P}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha}^{1/2}\mathbf{P}_{0}\right)\mathbf{D}_{0},

the matrix 𝚲0\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0} is nonsingular and diagonal, and 𝐀0=𝐀𝐏0​𝚲0\mathbf{A}_{0}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}.

Since

𝐇^−1→𝑝𝐇−1and𝐕^loc→𝑝𝐕0,\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{H}^{-1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{V}_{0},

we obtain

𝐀^loc→𝑝𝐀𝐏0​𝚲0.\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}.

For the root-NN expansion, write

𝐀^loc−𝐀0=(𝐇^−1−𝐇−1)​𝐕0+𝐇−1​(𝐕^loc−𝐕0)+(𝐇^−1−𝐇−1)​(𝐕^loc−𝐕0).\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{A}_{0}={}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right)\mathbf{V}_{0}+\mathbf{H}^{-1}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{V}_{0}\right)+\left(\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right)\left(\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{V}_{0}\right).

The last term is Op​(N−1)O_{p}(N^{-1}) because both factors are Op(N−1/2)O_{p}(N^{-1/2}). Therefore,

vec(𝐀^loc−𝐀0)=(𝐕0⊤⊗𝐈2)vec(𝐇^−1−𝐇−1)+(𝐈2⊗𝐇−1)vec(𝐕^loc−𝐕0)+op(N−1/2).\displaystyle\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{A}_{0}\right)=\left(\mathbf{V}_{0}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{2}\right)\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right)+\left(\mathbf{I}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right)\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{V}_{0}\right)+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}).

Substituting (S3.13) and (S3.15) yields

vec(𝐀^loc−𝐀0)=𝐉A(𝝁^N−𝝁N)+op(N−1/2),\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{A}_{0}\right)=\mathbf{J}_{A}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}\right)+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}),

where

𝐉A=(𝐕0⊤⊗𝐈2)​𝐉H−1+(𝐈2⊗𝐇−1)​𝐉V.\displaystyle\mathbf{J}_{A}=\left(\mathbf{V}_{0}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{2}\right)\mathbf{J}_{H^{-1}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{H}^{-1}\right)\mathbf{J}_{V}. (S3.16)

Thus 𝐉A\mathbf{J}_{A} is precisely the Jacobian of the locally oriented H-JADE map from the population moment vector to 𝐀𝐏0​𝚲0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}.

Finally, by Lemma S2 and (S2.1),

N​(𝝁^N−𝝁N)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝛀).\sqrt{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega}\right).

Therefore, 𝚺A=𝐉A​𝛀​𝐉A⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}=\mathbf{J}_{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{J}_{A}^{\top}, which completes the proof. ∎

S3.8 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

By Proposition S2, on a fixed local signed-permutation branch, there exist a permutation matrix 𝐏0\mathbf{P}_{0} and a nonsingular diagonal matrix 𝚲0\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0} such that, with 𝐀0=𝐀𝐏0​𝚲0\mathbf{A}_{0}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}, we have

𝐀^loc→𝑝𝐀0\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{A}_{0} (S3.17)

and

N​vec⁡(𝐀^loc−𝐀0)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺A).\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}-\mathbf{A}_{0}\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}\right). (S3.18)

The causal-effect estimator does not depend on this choice of local orientation. Indeed, any two ICA representatives differ by right multiplication by a signed-permutation matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}. For each row permutation 𝐏π\mathbf{P}_{\pi}, there are another row permutation 𝐏π′\mathbf{P}_{\pi^{\prime}} and a nonsingular diagonal matrix 𝐃π\mathbf{D}_{\pi} such that 𝐏π​𝐒−1=𝐃π​𝐏π′\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\mathbf{S}^{-1}=\mathbf{D}_{\pi}\mathbf{P}_{\pi^{\prime}}. As 𝒩⁡(𝐃π​𝐌)=𝒩⁡(𝐌)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{D}_{\pi}\mathbf{M})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{M}) whenever the relevant diagonal entries are nonzero, applying the recovery rule to 𝐀^​𝐒\widehat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{S} gives exactly the same set of admissible causal candidates as applying it to the original 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}}. The stability-selected causal-effect estimate is consequently invariant to signed permutations. We may therefore analyse the locally oriented representative 𝐀^loc\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}} without changing the estimator 𝐁^\widehat{\mathbf{B}}.

Recall that

𝐖=𝐀−1=𝐈2−𝐁=(1−β12−β211).\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\beta_{12}\\ -\beta_{21}&1\end{pmatrix}.

Since 𝐀0−1=𝚲0−1​𝐏0⊤​𝐖\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{W}, the correct row permutation of 𝐀0−1\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1} is 𝐏0\mathbf{P}_{0}. Indeed,

𝐏0​𝐀0−1=𝐏0​𝚲0−1​𝐏0⊤​𝐖.\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}=\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{W}.

Define 𝚫0=𝐏0​𝚲0−1​𝐏0⊤\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}=\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{0}^{\top}. Because 𝚲0\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0} is nonsingular and diagonal, 𝚫0\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0} is also nonsingular and diagonal. Therefore, 𝐏0​𝐀0−1=𝚫0​𝐖\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}. Since the diagonal entries of 𝐖\mathbf{W} are equal to one, the diagonal entries of 𝚫0​𝐖\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W} are nonzero, and the row normalisation in (S1.2) gives

𝒩⁡(𝐏0​𝐀0−1)=𝒩⁡(𝚫0​𝐖)=𝐖.\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}\right)=\mathbf{W}.

Consequently, the candidate causal matrix associated with 𝐏0\mathbf{P}_{0} is

𝐈2−𝒩⁡(𝐏0​𝐀0−1)=𝐈2−𝐖=𝐁.\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}\right)=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{B}.

We first show that the stability-based procedure selects this row permutation with probability tending to one. Let

𝐉=(0110)\mathbf{J}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}

be the swap matrix. Since 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} contains only two elements, the alternative row permutation is 𝐉𝐏0\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0}. For the correctly ordered candidate, continuity of matrix inversion and (S3.17) imply

𝐏0​(𝐀^loc)−1→𝑝𝚫0​𝐖.\mathbf{P}_{0}(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}})^{-1}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}.

The diagonal entries of the limit are nonzero. Hence the correct candidate is well defined with probability tending to one, and

𝐁^​(𝐏0)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\mathbf{P}_{0}) =𝐈2−𝒩⁡(𝐏0​(𝐀^loc)−1)\displaystyle=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{P}_{0}(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}})^{-1}\right)
→𝑝𝐈2−𝒩⁡(𝚫0​𝐖)=𝐁.\displaystyle\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}\right)=\mathbf{B}.

Continuity of the off-diagonal product gives

|B^12​(𝐏0)​B^21​(𝐏0)|→𝑝|β12​β21|<1.\bigl|\widehat{B}_{12}(\mathbf{P}_{0})\widehat{B}_{21}(\mathbf{P}_{0})\bigr|\xrightarrow{p}|\beta_{12}\beta_{21}|<1. (S3.19)

Consider now the alternative row permutation. We have

𝐉𝐏0​𝐀0−1=𝐉​𝚫0​𝐖=(𝐉​𝚫0​𝐉)​𝐉𝐖.\displaystyle\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}=\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}=\left(\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{J}\right)\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}.

The matrix 𝐉​𝚫0​𝐉\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{J} is nonsingular and diagonal, so row normalisation removes it whenever the normalisation is well defined. Moreover,

𝐉𝐖=(−β2111−β12).\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}=\begin{pmatrix}-\beta_{21}&1\\ 1&-\beta_{12}\end{pmatrix}.

Suppose first that β12​β21≠0\beta_{12}\beta_{21}\neq 0. Then both diagonal entries of 𝐉𝐖\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W} are nonzero, and the candidate causal matrix under the swapped ordering is

𝐁swap\displaystyle\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{swap}} =𝐈2−𝒩⁡(𝐉𝐖)\displaystyle=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W})
=(01/β211/β120).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/\beta_{21}\\ 1/\beta_{12}&0\end{pmatrix}.

Since the swapped candidate is well defined with probability tending to one, its off-diagonal product satisfies

|B^12​(𝐉𝐏0)​B^21​(𝐉𝐏0)|→𝑝1|β12​β21|>1.\bigl|\widehat{B}_{12}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0})\widehat{B}_{21}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0})\bigr|\xrightarrow{p}\frac{1}{|\beta_{12}\beta_{21}|}>1.

Together with (S3.19), this shows that the correct ordering is the unique stable ordering with probability tending to one.

Suppose instead that β12​β21=0\beta_{12}\beta_{21}=0. At least one diagonal entry of 𝐉𝐖\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W} is then zero, whereas both off-diagonal entries are equal to one. To make the finite-sample behaviour explicit, set 𝐌^N=𝐉𝐏0​(𝐀^loc)−1\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{N}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0}(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}})^{-1}. Then 𝐌^N→𝑝𝐉​𝚫0​𝐖\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{N}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}. Write 𝚫0=diag⁡(δ1,δ2)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_{1},\delta_{2}), with δ1​δ2≠0\delta_{1}\delta_{2}\neq 0. The limiting matrix is

𝐉​𝚫0​𝐖=(−δ2​β21δ2δ1−δ1​β12).\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W}=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta_{2}\beta_{21}&\delta_{2}\\ \delta_{1}&-\delta_{1}\beta_{12}\end{pmatrix}.

Whenever the swapped candidate is well defined, its off-diagonal product satisfies

|B^12​(𝐉𝐏0)​B^21​(𝐉𝐏0)|=|M^N,12​M^N,21M^N,11​M^N,22|.\bigl|\widehat{B}_{12}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0})\widehat{B}_{21}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{0})\bigr|=\left|\frac{\widehat{M}_{N,12}\widehat{M}_{N,21}}{\widehat{M}_{N,11}\widehat{M}_{N,22}}\right|.

The numerator converges in probability to δ1​δ2≠0\delta_{1}\delta_{2}\neq 0, whereas the denominator converges in probability to δ1​δ2​β12​β21=0\delta_{1}\delta_{2}\beta_{12}\beta_{21}=0. Consequently, for any fixed K>0K>0, the probability that the swapped candidate is both well defined and has an off-diagonal product of absolute value at most KK tends to zero. If one of the relevant sample diagonal entries is exactly zero, the swapped candidate is excluded from the admissible set by (S1.3). Thus, in either event, it cannot be selected over the correctly ordered candidate with asymptotic probability bounded away from zero.

Combining the two cases, the row ordering 𝐏^loc\widehat{\mathbf{P}}^{\mathrm{loc}} selected from the locally oriented mixing matrix satisfies

ℙ⁡(𝐏^loc=𝐏0)⟶1.\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{P}}^{\mathrm{loc}}=\mathbf{P}_{0}\right)\longrightarrow 1. (S3.20)

We next study the causal recovery map locally around 𝐀0\mathbf{A}_{0}. Define

𝒢𝐏0​(𝐌~)=𝐈2−𝒩⁡(𝐏0​𝐌~−1).\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}})=\mathbf{I}_{2}-\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{P}_{0}\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}^{-1}).

Since 𝐀0\mathbf{A}_{0} is nonsingular and the diagonal entries of 𝐏0​𝐀0−1=𝚫0​𝐖\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W} are nonzero, 𝒢𝐏0\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}} is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of 𝐀0\mathbf{A}_{0}. Furthermore, 𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀0)=𝐁\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}(\mathbf{A}_{0})=\mathbf{B}. On the event {𝐏^loc=𝐏0}\{\widehat{\mathbf{P}}^{\mathrm{loc}}=\mathbf{P}_{0}\}, 𝐁^=𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀^loc)\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\right). Together with (S3.20) and (S3.17), this proves 𝐁^→𝑝𝐁\widehat{\mathbf{B}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf{B}.

The derivative of the causal recovery map is as follows. For a matrix 𝐊∈ℝ2×2\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, define 𝒟⁡(𝐊)=diag⁡(K11,K22)\mathscr{D}(\mathbf{K})=\operatorname{diag}(K_{11},K_{22}). The derivative of the row-normalisation map at 𝐌0=𝚫0​𝐖\mathbf{M}_{0}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}\mathbf{W} in the direction 𝐊\mathbf{K} is

D​𝒩​(𝐌0)​[𝐊]=𝚫0−1​𝐊−𝚫0−1​𝒟​(𝐊)​𝐖.D\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{M}_{0})[\mathbf{K}]=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{K}-\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}^{-1}\mathscr{D}(\mathbf{K})\mathbf{W}. (S3.21)

Indeed, writing

𝒩⁡(𝐌~)={𝒟⁡(𝐌~)}−1​𝐌~\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}})=\{\mathscr{D}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}})\}^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}

and differentiating the inverse of the diagonal matrix 𝒟⁡(𝐌~)\mathscr{D}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}) gives (S3.21).

For a matrix perturbation 𝐅\mathbf{F}, the derivative of matrix inversion at 𝐀0\mathbf{A}_{0} maps 𝐅\mathbf{F} to −𝐀0−1​𝐅𝐀0−1-\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{F}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}. Define 𝐊⁡(𝐅)=𝐏0​𝐀0−1​𝐅𝐀0−1\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{F})=\mathbf{P}_{0}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{F}\mathbf{A}_{0}^{-1}. The negative sign in the derivative of the inverse cancels with the negative sign in the definition of 𝒢𝐏0\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}. Hence

D​𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀0)​[𝐅]=𝚫0−1​𝐊​(𝐅)−𝚫0−1​𝒟​{𝐊⁡(𝐅)}​𝐖.\displaystyle D\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}(\mathbf{A}_{0})[\mathbf{F}]=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{F})-\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{0}^{-1}\mathscr{D}\left\{\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{F})\right\}\mathbf{W}. (S3.22)

Let 𝐉B\mathbf{J}_{B} denote the matrix representation of the linear map in (S3.22), so that

vec⁡{D​𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀0)​[𝐅]}=𝐉B​vec⁡(𝐅).\operatorname{vec}\left\{D\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}(\mathbf{A}_{0})[\mathbf{F}]\right\}=\mathbf{J}_{B}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{F}).

This is the Jacobian of the causal recovery map evaluated at the correctly scaled and permuted mixing matrix 𝐀0=𝐀𝐏0​𝚲0\mathbf{A}_{0}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{0}.

The multivariate delta method applied to (S3.18) now gives

N​vec⁡[𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀^loc)−𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀0)]→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝐉B​𝚺A​𝐉B⊤).\displaystyle\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{vec}\left[\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\right)-\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}(\mathbf{A}_{0})\right]\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{J}_{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}\mathbf{J}_{B}^{\top}\right).

By (S3.20) and the signed-permutation invariance established above, 𝐁^=𝒢𝐏0​(𝐀^loc)\widehat{\mathbf{B}}=\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{P}_{0}}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{A}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\right) with probability tending to one. Therefore replacing the locally fixed candidate by the stability-selected estimator does not affect its limiting distribution. It follows that

N​vec⁡(𝐁^−𝐁)→𝑑ℕ⁡(𝟎,𝚺B),\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{vec}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}-\mathbf{B}\right)\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B}\right),

where 𝚺B=𝐉B​𝚺A​𝐉B⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B}=\mathbf{J}_{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}\mathbf{J}_{B}^{\top}. Let 𝐄β\mathbf{E}_{\beta} extract the entries (B12,B21)⊤(B_{12},B_{21})^{\top} from vec⁡(𝐁)\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{B}). Since 𝚺A=𝐉A​𝛀​𝐉A⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}=\mathbf{J}_{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{J}_{A}^{\top}, the delta method gives 𝚺β=𝐉β​𝛀​𝐉β⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\beta}=\mathbf{J}_{\beta}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{J}_{\beta}^{\top}, where 𝐉β=𝐄β​𝐉B​𝐉A\mathbf{J}_{\beta}=\mathbf{E}_{\beta}\mathbf{J}_{B}\mathbf{J}_{A}, which is the covariance representation stated in Theorem 2. This completes the proof. ∎

S3.9 Proof of Proposition 2

Proof.

Write 𝐛^=vec⁡(𝐁^)\widehat{\mathbf{b}}=\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}), 𝐛^∗=vec⁡(𝐁^∗)\widehat{\mathbf{b}}^{*}=\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\mathbf{B}}^{*}), and 𝐛=vec⁡(𝐁)\mathbf{b}=\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{B}). and

𝜽N=N−1​∑j=1N𝐪j,N.\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{q}_{j,N}.

The corrected H-JADE moment vector is 𝝁^N=𝚽⁡(𝜽^N)\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{N}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{N}), with population value 𝝁N=𝚽⁡(𝜽N)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{N}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}). Let 𝐆N=D​𝚽​(𝜽N)\mathbf{G}_{N}=D\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{N}) and 𝐦j,N=𝐆N​𝐯j,N\mathbf{m}_{j,N}=\mathbf{G}_{N}\mathbf{v}_{j,N}. Then 𝔼⁡(𝐦j,N)=𝟎\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{m}_{j,N})=\mathbf{0}, and (S2.1) is the long-run covariance of {𝐦j,N}\{\mathbf{m}_{j,N}\}.

S4 Additional simulation results and diagnostics

This section gives implementation details and additional numerical results for Section 5.

S4.1 Primary simulations

The summary-data standard errors were generated on the standardised-genotype scale as 1/neff,j​k​qj1/\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff},jk}q_{j}}, where neff,j​kn_{\mathrm{eff},jk} is the variant- and trait-specific effective sample size and qjq_{j} is the information score. H-JADE used 200 moving-block-bootstrap replications. The four direction-specific comparators used the same p<10−5p<10^{-5} selection threshold and r2<0.001r^{2}<0.001 clumping rule; MR-RAPS used over-dispersion with Huber loss.

Bias, SD, CP and average confidence-interval length are calculated over 200 Monte Carlo replications. All methods returned a point estimate and interval in every primary replication. Table S1 compares the Monte Carlo standard deviations with the average H-JADE bootstrap standard errors for both NN. The two measures are generally close, supporting the use of the moving block bootstrap for standard error estimation.

Tables S2 and S3 report the corresponding estimation and interval results at N=2000N=2000. The results show broadly similar patterns to those at N=5000N=5000, with greater estimation variability and generally longer confidence intervals at N=2000N=2000.

S4.2 Directional testing comparison

We applied the released Focused-main.R implementation of Li and Ye, (2025) to the same simulated summary data. For each direction, variants were screened at exposure-association p<0.05p<0.05; variants with p≤10−5p\leq 10^{-5} were eligible as clumping index variants, and clumping required pairwise r2≤0.001r^{2}\leq 0.001 within the simulated LD blocks. The reverse direction used the same procedure after exchanging the two traits. For a post-clumping candidate panel of size psp_{s}, the focused set satisfies

|γ^out|se⁡(γ^out)≤τf,|γ^exp|se⁡(γ^exp)≥τs,τs=Φ−1​(1−1/ps).\frac{|\widehat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{out}}|}{\operatorname{se}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{out}})}\leq\tau_{f},\qquad\frac{|\widehat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{exp}}|}{\operatorname{se}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{exp}})}\geq\tau_{s},\qquad\tau_{s}=\Phi^{-1}(1-1/p_{s}).

We used Fo-IVW with τf=1.2\tau_{f}=1.2 and 1.5 and Fo-Median with τf=1.5\tau_{f}=1.5; Fo-Median used 300 bootstrap resamples. The released routine was used without modifying its treatment of focused sets containing at most two variants.

Table S4 reports the rejection rates for all settings and both causal directions, including the null cases excluded from Figure 1. Setting 1R is Setting 1 with the two directional effects interchanged, (β12,β21)=(0.5,0)(\beta_{12},\beta_{21})=(0.5,0).

S4.3 Point-estimation comparison with LHC-MR

Each data set contained 5000 input variants. We used the likelihood point-estimation stage of the publicly available LHC-MR implementation, with nStep = 2, SP_single = 3, SP_pair = 50, and SNP_filter = 10. The resulting pair analysis retained 500 variants. H-JADE was fitted both to these same 500 variants and to the full 5000-variant panel. LHC-MR block-jackknife inference was not run in this comparison.

The independent-source scenario used independent trait-specific genetic sources. The shared-heritable-component scenario additionally included the shared source in the LHC-MR model. The generating causal effects were (β12,β21)=(−0.4,0.5)(\beta_{12},\beta_{21})=(-0.4,0.5). Table S5 reports all five data sets in each scenario; “Full” and “Matched” denote H-JADE fitted to the full and retained panels, respectively.

The 50-start likelihood optimisation dominated the LHC-MR running time. Median end-to-end point-estimation times were 7.94 and 7.84 hours in the two considered scenarios. Median H-JADE point-fit times were 0.30 and 0.45 seconds on the full panels and 0.01 and 0.03 seconds on the matched panels. These timings exclude H-JADE moving-block-bootstrap inference and LHC-MR block-jackknife inference.

S4.4 Sensitivity to local dependence

Within each LD block, the trait-kk direct effects were generated as

αj​k=∑h=05ch​(θk)​εj−h,k,ch​(θ)=θh{∑r=05θ2​r}1/2,\alpha_{jk}=\sum_{h=0}^{5}c_{h}(\theta_{k})\varepsilon_{j-h,k},\qquad c_{h}(\theta)=\frac{\theta^{h}}{\{\sum_{r=0}^{5}\theta^{2r}\}^{1/2}},

where {εj​k}j=1N\{\varepsilon_{jk}\}_{j=1}^{N} are independent innovations following the same two-component Gaussian mixture as the primitive direct effects in primary Setting 6. The process was restarted independently at each LD-block boundary, with pre-block innovations generated to preserve the marginal variance near the boundary. The two innovation sequences were independent. Within each Monte Carlo replication, the same primitive innovations and GWAS noise were used across the four dependence configurations. The case (θ1,θ2)=(0,0)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=(0,0) agrees with primary Setting 6 replication by replication.

This construction departs from the covariance equalisation obtained under independent primitive direct effects. Writing 𝐬j=ℓj−1/2∑r=1NRj​r𝜶r⋅\mathbf{s}_{j}=\ell_{j}^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^{N}R_{jr}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{r\cdot}, the MA(5) dependence gives

Cov⁡(𝐬j)=𝐃j=diag⁡{σα,12​fj​1,σα,22​fj​2},\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{s}_{j})=\mathbf{D}_{j}=\operatorname{diag}\{\sigma_{\alpha,1}^{2}f_{j1},\sigma_{\alpha,2}^{2}f_{j2}\},

where

fj​k=1ℓj​σα,k2​∑r=1N∑q=1NRj​r​Rj​q​Cov⁡(αr​k,αq​k)f_{jk}=\frac{1}{\ell_{j}\sigma_{\alpha,k}^{2}}\sum_{r=1}^{N}\sum_{q=1}^{N}R_{jr}R_{jq}\operatorname{Cov}(\alpha_{rk},\alpha_{qk})

measures the change in source variance induced by local dependence and LD; under independent primitive effects, fj​k=1f_{jk}=1. Thus 𝐃j\mathbf{D}_{j} is no longer the common matrix 𝐃α\mathbf{D}_{\alpha} used in the primary model. Because the two source processes remain independent, each 𝐃j\mathbf{D}_{j} is diagonal and 𝐃¯=N−1​∑j𝐃j\overline{\mathbf{D}}=N^{-1}\sum_{j}\mathbf{D}_{j} remains diagonal. Hence the average signal covariance has the form 𝐑s=𝐀​𝐃¯​𝐀⊤\mathbf{R}_{s}=\mathbf{A}\overline{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{A}^{\top}, so whitening based on 𝐑s\mathbf{R}_{s} still orthogonalises the common mixing directions. What is lost is the rowwise standardisation: 𝐃¯−1/2𝐬j\overline{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\mathbf{s}_{j} has a variant-specific diagonal covariance rather than 𝐈2\mathbf{I}_{2}. The fourth-order correction derived under common source covariance is therefore no longer exact, and the serial dependence also changes the long-run variability of the sample moment estimators.

Table S6 summarises the induced departure at N=5000N=5000. The variance factor is the average of fj​kf_{jk} across variants. The strongest first-source setting has lag-one correlation 0.767, while the correlation between the two aggregated source processes remains close to zero. As θ1\theta_{1} increases from 0 to 0.8, the first-source variance factor rises from 1.00 to 3.37 and its excess kurtosis falls from 17.31 to 5.64. These two changes work in different directions: positive MA dependence combined with positive LD increases the variance of the aggregated genetic signal, while the moving average makes the source less strongly non-Gaussian. When (θ1,θ2)=(0.5,0.5)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=(0.5,0.5), the two variance-factor profiles are identical across variants; at (0.8,0.5)(0.8,0.5), their ratio has coefficient of variation 0.147. The source-specific part of the rowwise scaling departure is therefore smaller than the raw serial correlations alone suggest. The median whitening condition number was 1.58 at (0,0)(0,0) and 2.37 at (0.8,0.5)(0.8,0.5).

S5 Additional real-data information

S5.1 GWAS sources

Table S7 lists the five GWAS datasets used in the LDL-C–CHD, ApoB–CHD and TG–T2D applications. All three lipid GWAS were conducted in UK Biobank; the CHD and strict T2D GWAS came from FinnGen. Each trait pair therefore combines UK Biobank with FinnGen summary statistics, limiting the scope for sample overlap between the two GWAS in that pair. The original GWAS sample sizes are reported below.

S5.2 Estimation procedures and complete results

For H-JADE, alleles were harmonised between the two GWAS and variants with incompatible alleles were removed. The harmonised variants were then matched to a European-ancestry LD-score reference (Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015a, ; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015b, ).

The GWAS-VCF associations and standard errors are reported per effect allele. For SNP jj, let fjf_{j} denote its allele frequency in the European genotype reference and define dj={2​fj​(1−fj)}1/2d_{j}=\{2f_{j}(1-f_{j})\}^{1/2}. After matching the reference and harmonised allele pairs, the same djd_{j} was applied to both traits:

x^j​k=dj​Γ^j​kℓj,σ~j​k=dj​σ^j​kℓj,k∈{1,2}.\widehat{x}_{jk}=\frac{d_{j}\widehat{\Gamma}_{jk}}{\sqrt{\ell_{j}}},\qquad\widetilde{\sigma}_{jk}=\frac{d_{j}\widehat{\sigma}_{jk}}{\sqrt{\ell_{j}}},\qquad k\in\{1,2\}. (S5.1)

Here ℓj\ell_{j} is the LD score, and Γ^j​k\widehat{\Gamma}_{jk} and σ^j​k\widehat{\sigma}_{jk} denote the per-allele GWAS association estimate and its standard error. The resulting noise-covariance diagonal entries are σ~j​k2\widetilde{\sigma}_{jk}^{2}. This conversion changes the genotype unit without altering the phenotype-specific outcome scales. Cross-trait sampling-error covariances were set to zero, reflecting the use of distinct GWAS cohorts. H-JADE used the resulting variant-specific noise covariances in its second- and fourth-order moment corrections.

Standard errors for H-JADE were estimated using 200 chromosome-stratified moving block bootstrap replications, with block length round⁡(3​N1/3)\operatorname{round}(3N^{1/3}) for a final panel of NN SNPs. Two-sided pp-values and 95% confidence intervals were calculated from a normal approximation using the bootstrap standard deviation. The four direction-specific estimators (IVW, MR-Egger, MR-RAPS and the weighted median) were fitted separately for each exposure–outcome ordering. Exposure-associated variants with p<10−5p<10^{-5} were clumped against the European reference (r2=0.001r^{2}=0.001, 10,000 kb), followed by allele harmonisation. MR-RAPS used its default settings (over-dispersion, Huber loss and no shrinkage). Table S8 provides the estimates and corresponding inference for all six directions.

S5.3 Focusing comparison

We applied the Fo-IVW and Fo-Median tests using the implementation of Li and Ye, (2025). For each exposure–outcome ordering, variants with exposure-association pp-values below 0.05 were entered into PLINK clumping (10,000 kb; r2=0.001r^{2}=0.001), with clump index variants required to have p≤10−5p\leq 10^{-5}. The candidate set comprised the index SNPs with available, allele-harmonised outcome associations. Outcome data were matched by SNP identifier, without proxies.

Let ncandn_{\mathrm{cand}} denote the number of candidates for a given direction. Following the published implementation, the strong-instrument threshold was τs=Φ−1​(1−ncand−1)\tau_{s}=\Phi^{-1}(1-n_{\mathrm{cand}}^{-1}). We used τf∈{1.2,1.5}\tau_{f}\in\{1.2,1.5\} for Fo-IVW and τf=1.5\tau_{f}=1.5 for Fo-Median. For the latter, we set weight.order = -1 and used 10,000 null bootstrap replicates. The focused sets were determined by the exposure- and outcome-association thresholds described in Supplementary Section S4.2. Table S9 gives the corresponding set sizes and test pp-values.
